Effective management of open-source software (OSS) vulnerabilities is now a critical task, particularly given the increasing number of newly discovered vulnerabilities. To prevent exploitation, the standard process includes monitoring commits that fix vulnerabilities, which can, however, be time-consuming to review manually. To address this issue, machine learning-based solutions have been proposed to automatically detect vulnerability-fixing commits, although most have limitations in their approach. This paper introduces VulCurator, a tool that utilizes deep learning to classify vulnerability-fixing commits based on a comprehensive range of information, such as commit messages, code modifications, and issue reports. The results of the experiment demonstrate that VulCurator significantly outperforms existing benchmarks, achieving a higher F1-score of up to 16.1%. The VulCurator tool is openly available for public access, along with a demo video and additional documentation.

Recently, a modified jet algorithm, flavoured anti-$k_{\text{T}}$, was proposed and we have applied it to the study of $Wb\bar{b}$ production at the 8 TeV Large Hadron Collider. Our results for the total cross section and differential distributions are presented at the next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD. The impact of the flavoured anti-$k_{\text{T}}$ algorithm's remaining adjustable parameters and its performance in comparison to the standard flavour-$k_{\text{T}}$ algorithm are discussed. Our total cross section predictions are in good agreement with the CMS data, and the inclusion of the significant NNLO QCD corrections substantially improves the agreement.

Relativistic magnetic reconnections are common in the universe and in many cases, the surrounding plasma rapidly cools due to the emission of synchrotron radiation. We analyzed a specific situation where the energy in the magnetic field is extremely high, the density of the system is moderate, and the energy in the magnetic field and the energy in the particles are in a delicate balance. This balance leads to the production of pairs of electrons and their antiparticles, which in turn affects the strength of the magnetic field. Our study revealed a stable balance between the energy in the magnetic field and the energy in the particles, which can be useful in systems where the density of the particles is not well understood. This balance can be applied to study the properties of the universe, such as the current sheets near a supermassive black hole in the galaxy M87 and the current sheets near a pulsar, like the Crab pulsar.

We analyzed the internal movements of the young star-forming area NGC 346 in the Small Magellanic Cloud using two sets of 11-year-apart, in-depth images from the Hubble Space Telescope. Our study focused on the movements of various populations, which we identified based on their color, brightness, and spatial patterns. The movements of the young stars in NGC 346 revealed intricate patterns, and the upper-main sequence and pre-main sequence stars exhibited similar movements. The outer areas of the cluster showed a mix of outward and inward movements, while the central areas displayed a combination of rotation and inward motion, reaching speeds of approximately 3 and 1 kilometers per second, respectively. Our findings suggest that turbulence drives star formation in NGC 346. The similar movements we observed in NGC 346 and the star-forming areas of the Milky Way indicate that differences in metal content and dust density between the two galaxies have a minimal impact on star cluster assembly and growth. Our results are consistent with the proposed star cluster formation models.

Program code names exhibit significant variation, influenced by individual developer preferences, resulting in inconsistent and sometimes contradictory nomenclature. This makes name comparison challenging, requiring a precise yet flexible matching process that accounts for word variations, order reconfigurations, and semantic similarities. To facilitate such comparison, we have developed a library of specialized functions designed to evaluate the similarity between code names, allowing researchers to select the most suitable method for their specific needs. These functions balance lexical matching with the nuances of human perception, aiming to reflect the subtleties of name similarity.

This paper presents a formula for the $n$th term of a $k$-generalized Fibonacci sequence, a broader class of sequences encompassing the standard Fibonacci sequence, which starts with $k$ arbitrary initial values and continues by adding the previous $k$ terms. The derived formula was achieved by analyzing patterns in the sequences of the Fibonacci, Tribonacci, and Tetrabonacci types, and the formula for the general case was also developed to aid in the proof of the paper's central result.

Graph artificial intelligence (graph AI) has seen significant advancements in modeling intricate systems, spanning across various fields such as biology and physics. The growing diversity of graph datasets necessitates the development of multimodal techniques capable of incorporating multiple inductive biases. These inductive biases, which serve as the foundation for algorithms' predictive abilities, can differ across various data modalities and are often not explicitly provided in the input. To overcome these challenges, researchers have devised multimodal graph AI methods that seamlessly integrate disparate modalities while accounting for cross-modal relationships. Our comprehensive survey of 145 graph AI studies reveals a growing trend of utilizing diverse datasets, which are then fed into sophisticated multimodal models. These models can be broadly categorized into image-intensive, knowledge-grounded, and language-intensive types. Based on this categorization, we have developed a framework to analyze existing methods and guide the development of future multimodal graph AI techniques.

Nonlinear conservation laws present considerable challenges in the context of adjoint-based optimization, specifically concerning the existence and uniqueness of both the direct and adjoint solutions, and the overall well-posedness of the problem for gradient-based optimization algorithms. This paper aims to examine the convergence of the adjoint equations to known exact solutions of the inviscid Burgers' equation using various numerical schemes. The study will also investigate the impact of the non-differentiability of the approximate Riemann solver, the method of differentiating the discrete schemes, and inconsistencies in time-stepping.

A small, spheroid-shaped object moving actively in a stationary fluid experiences a torque, which causes it to align in a way that facilitates settling, typically by presenting its widest side first. It's found that a similar torque occurs in the case of an active particle settling in a fluid at rest. The torque experienced by a spherical, swimming particle, known as a squirmer, is determined by the formula $\boldsymbol{T}^\prime = -{\tfrac{9}{8}} m_f (\boldsymbol{v}_s^{(0)} \wedge \boldsymbol{v}_g^{(0)})$, where the variables have the same meaning. This torque causes the particle's swimming direction to oppose the force of gravity, leading to a stable upward motion and unstable downward motion.

This study examines the present stability of bosonic superconducting cosmic strings, which are typically plagued by quantum instability due to non-zero string curvature. The decay rates of the current-carrying particles are calculated using various model parameters, curved string configurations, and decay mechanisms. The cosmological implications of superconducting string networks and cosmic vortons are also investigated by tracing their evolutionary paths. The results reveal that, in certain scenarios, the zero-mode vortons cannot maintain stability, especially in cases where the mass of the current-carrying particle differs significantly from the string tension, or where the particle interacts strongly with lighter species like the Standard Model particles.

We have conducted a study using circularly polarized and longitudinal light to investigate the magnetic field induced Hofstadter butterfly in a single-twist trilayer graphene. The results show that the equilibrium state of the trilayer graphene exhibits two distinct chiral limits and a bifurcation in the central branch of the Hofstadter butterfly. The addition of circularly polarized light significantly alters the butterfly's energy spectrum by creating a substantial gap and demonstrating a clear asymmetry at zero energy. Furthermore, the effect of circularly polarized light was found to vary depending on its handedness, causing the central band to shift downward in the case of right-handed light and upward in the case of left-handed light. Conversely, the effect of longitudinally polarized light, originating from a waveguide, was discovered to break the chiral symmetry of the Hofstadter butterfly at low driving strengths, only to restore it at higher strengths, a phenomenon contrasting the behavior of twisted bilayer graphene.

Compounds with noncentrosymmetric structures have garnered significant interest due to their potential to exhibit unconventional superconductivity. NbIr$_2$B$_2$ is a new compound in this class, displaying superconductivity at a temperature of 7.3(2) Kelvin and a remarkably high upper critical field beyond the Pauli limit. This study presents the findings of muon spin rotation experiments, which examined the temperature and magnetic field dependence of the magnetic penetration depth in NbIr$_2$B$_2$. The results of the transverse-field muon spin rotation indicate a fully gapped s-wave superconductivity, and the estimated upper critical field is also supported by high-field transport measurements. Notably, the ratio of the superconducting transition temperature to the magnetic penetration depth squared in NbIr$_2$B$_2$ is similar to that of unconventional superconductors. Furthermore, zero-field muon spin rotation data shows no notable change in the muon spin relaxation rate above and below the superconducting transition temperature, suggesting that time-reversal symmetry is preserved in the superconducting state. The results of this study are expected to prompt theoretical investigations to understand the microscopic origin of superconductivity in this unique noncentrosymmetric system.

We are driven by the potential of our findings in the realms of distributed storage, computation, and homomorphic secret sharing to develop efficient communication strategies. This involves the creation of low-bandwidth schemes to calculate the weighted sums of multiple encoded data points, where we have partial access to the remaining encoded data. 

Given a codeword in a Reed-Solomon code, we are tasked with evaluating the weighted sum of a subset of encoded data, and we propose a novel approach to accomplish this by downloading a limited number of data sub-components from available nodes, provided we have enough nodes to satisfy a certain condition. This approach often surpasses existing solutions in the literature. 

We also present a broader framework for evaluating linear combinations of encoded data, and by applying this framework to the case of Reed-Solomon codes, we are able to establish a lower bound for the communication requirements.

Researchers have become increasingly interested in high-entropy alloys due to their impressive mechanical properties and the vast possibilities they offer. However, the complex composition of these alloys poses a challenge to both theoretical modeling and the development of macro-scale models, making it difficult to accurately simulate their behavior. Machine learning offers a solution to these challenges by its ability to capture complex relationships. This review aims to explore the potential of machine learning in overcoming the obstacles associated with high-entropy alloys. It begins by providing a foundation in machine learning algorithms and their applications, and then discusses the latest models being used to simulate the behavior of these alloys. The focus is placed on the prediction of phase behavior, the calculation of defects, and the simulation of plastic deformation. The review also covers the application of machine learning to the study of macro-scale properties, such as lattice structures, phase formation, and mechanical properties. Examples are provided to illustrate the potential of machine-learned phase-formation rules and order parameters. The discussion concludes by highlighting the remaining challenges and presenting potential future research directions, including the development of more robust models and the application of machine learning to the inverse design of materials.

The non-relativistic warm dark matter particle velocity dispersion scales inversely with the universe's expansion parameter, where the dispersion results in a free-streaming cut-off of the density fluctuations' power spectrum. The free-streaming wavenumber at the time of matter-radiation equality was estimated to be in the range of 2.0 to 3.8 Mpc^-1, while the corresponding velocity dispersion was between 0.29 and 0.67 km/s, both at 68% confidence. This result supports the reionization scenario. The free-streaming cut-off also yields the constraints of a velocity dispersion less than 0.67 km/s and a wavenumber greater than 1.5 Mpc^-1. These constraints are in agreement with previous measurements from galaxy rotation curves and the formation of the first galaxies. The derived temperature-to-mass ratio of warm dark matter matches the no freeze-in and no freeze-out scenario of spin 0 dark matter decoupling early from the standard model sector. This scenario disfavors spin 1/2 and spin 1 dark matter. A theoretical model featuring scalar dark matter and a scalar sector in the standard model of quarks and leptons, in agreement with the constraints, is presented. Discrepancies with dark matter mass limits in the literature are also discussed.

We develop a fluctuation algebra framework for fermions in a state of approximate free behavior and determine its time-evolution for approximately free dynamics. Additionally, we investigate a Bose-Einstein condensate and assess its stability in the presence of interactions.

Scientific computations heavily rely on linear algebra expressions, often computed using a sequence of pre-existing library functions. This sequence represents a computational strategy, where multiple algorithms exist for a single linear algebra expression, despite being mathematically equivalent. However, the algorithms' performance can vary significantly, particularly in terms of execution time. Several high-level languages and tools, like Julia and Armadillo, select algorithms by minimizing Floating Point Operations (FLOPs). Nonetheless, algorithms with the same or similar FLOP counts can exhibit different execution times, making one choice seemingly arbitrary. Conversely, the algorithm minimizing FLOPs is not always the one minimizing execution time. This study develops a method to assess the reliability of FLOPs in distinguishing between linear algebra algorithms. The approach ranks algorithms into performance classes, allowing multiple algorithms to share the same rank, by iteratively measuring their performance until the ranks stabilize. If the algorithms with the minimum FLOPs are assigned the top rank, the FLOP count is considered a valid performance discriminator; otherwise, the instance is flagged as an anomaly, aiding in the identification of the root cause of performance discrepancies.

We offer a theoretical framework and numerical assessments of the backscattering rate influenced by acceptor holes or Mn spins in HgTe and (Hg,Mn)Te quantum wells operating in the quantum spin Hall regime. The contributions of s-p and sp-d exchange interactions, Kondo coupling, Luttinger liquid effects, precessional dephasing, and bound magnetic polarons are systematically examined. The calculated conductance values and temperature dependence are found to match the experimental data for HgTe and (Hg,Mn)Te quantum wells.

The contextual bandit problem, a widely applicable theoretical framework, typically assumes noise and contexts are independent. However, our research considers a more practical scenario where noise, a latent confounding factor, influences both contexts and rewards. This more realistic setting, though making the problem more complex, expands the potential applications. Nevertheless, unresolved confounding variables in the model lead to biased reward estimations and significant regret. To overcome this, we utilize the dual instrumental variable regression, which accurately identifies the true reward function. Theoretical analysis shows our approach achieves a near-optimal convergence rate in two commonly used reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. Consequently, we develop computationally efficient and regret-optimal algorithms for the confounded bandit problem, validated by numerical results demonstrating the effectiveness of our methods in the confounded bandit setting.

We have previously demonstrated that the minimal symplectic fillings of oriented lens spaces, equipped with their canonical contact structures, can be generated from the minimal resolution of their underlying singularities via a sequence of symplectic blowdowns. This time, we present a significantly more straightforward representation of our blowdown process, using the triangulations of a convex polygon. As a result, we are able to categorize the symplectic deformation equivalence classes of minimal symplectic fillings of a given lens space into a connected, directed, and graded graph, where the starting point is the minimal resolution of the corresponding singularity and each edge represents a symplectic blowdown. We also establish a bound on the number of steps required to achieve each symplectic filling.

The generation of efficient paths in challenging dynamic environments remains a persistent challenge in the unmanned surface vehicle (USV) field. This paper proposes a cooperative trajectory planning algorithm for a coupled USV-UAV system to ensure a USV's safe and smooth navigation in obstacle-ridden areas. The unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) acts as a real-time sensor, providing a global map and obstacle data via a lightweight semantic segmentation network and 3D transformation. The system generates an initial trajectory using a graph-based search method, and incorporates a numerical optimization approach to account for the USV's unique kinematic constraints. The final motion control method employs a nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) approach, prioritizing energy efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the system, yielding a locally optimal trajectory with high tracking accuracy for the USV.

Autonomous underwater surface vessels are extensively applied in the areas of oceanic discovery and environmental preservation. In order to guarantee the success of a USV mission, two essential technologies are needed: trajectory mapping and motion tracking. This paper introduces a new, optimised approach to generating and tracking a USV's path, founded on the principles of optimisation. The dynamic model of the USV is initially outlined in a differential flatness format, enabling the creation of a linear, system-based path using the dynamic Rapidly-exploring Random Tree* algorithm. The number of data points needed to achieve the desired path is minimised and computational efficiency enhanced by implementing local optimisation. Furthermore, the optimisation process considers the dynamic constraints, resulting in a path that accurately reflects the kinematic properties of the under-actuated hull, making it simpler to track. The motion tracking process is further enhanced by the implementation of model predictive control, utilising a sequential quadratic programming problem. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the planned path, which closely aligns with the kinematic characteristics of the USV, and the tracking accuracy remains at a high level.

Financial transactions rely heavily on currency, and in many African nations, physical cash is the primary medium of exchange. Ethiopia, one of the world's nations with the highest rates of blindness and low vision, struggles to facilitate everyday financial dealings. Approximately 4 million citizens are visually impaired, with 1.7 million suffering complete vision loss. This population encounters significant challenges in daily activities, including navigating public areas where money exchanges are necessary. This research proposes a solution to address this issue by leveraging AI and machine learning technologies. An innovative mobile application, designed to operate on both Android and iOS platforms, was developed, featuring a model that achieved a classification accuracy of 98.9% in testing. The application incorporates a voice-activated feature, offering the scanned currency's identification in Amharic, the predominant language in Ethiopia. The application prioritizes accessibility, aiming to alleviate the difficulties faced by visually impaired individuals in Ethiopia.

The role of vortices in planet formation, where they accumulate dust in pressure maxima, remains a subject of inquiry, particularly the stability of vortices collecting dust and the circumstances of their breakup. Our investigation into this phenomenon utilized high-resolution two-dimensional simulations of dust-laden vortices in protoplanetary discs. By leveraging the terminal velocity approximation in a local shearing box, we were able to efficiently simulate the dynamics of dust in the gas. Our findings reveal that the stability of two-dimensional dust-laden vortices in protoplanetary discs hinges on their size relative to the disc's scale height and the degree of dust coupling. Our simulations indicate that smaller vortices, whose minor axis is significantly smaller than the scale height, are stable for extended periods. In contrast, larger vortices, whose minor axis approaches the scale height, exhibit a drag instability following a prolonged contraction phase, resulting in the core becoming increasingly enriched with dust. The lifetime of these vortices depends on the size of the dust grains, with larger grains precipitating the instability sooner. Our results imply that the stability of vortices, either those formed by vertical shear instability and zombie vortex instability or those larger vortices disrupted by hydrodynamic instabilities, is influenced by the presence of dust in the disc. Moreover, the observed lifetimes, though shortened by the presence of dust in larger vortices, were sufficient to facilitate considerable dust enrichment in the vortex cores.

Over the past few years, machine learning potentials (MLP) have gained significant interest in the fields of chemistry and materials science. The main objective of many recent advancements in MLP is to replicate the precision of electronic structure calculations in large systems comprised of thousands of atoms. However, the reliability of contemporary MLPs in reproducing the intricate specifics of the multi-dimensional potential-energy surface in such systems remains a challenge to assess. Conversely, smaller systems suitable for thorough quality-control assessments are less commonly studied. This research leverages high-quality harmonic and anharmonic vibrational frequencies as a precise validation tool for high-dimensional neural network potentials. Specifically, the formic acid dimer, a well-established model system, was analyzed to demonstrate the capability of state-of-the-art calculations to yield accurate frequencies in alignment with coupled cluster theory and experimental data.

The complexities of human anatomy, form, and related illnesses can be studied using medical images, but accessing this data is hindered by privacy, data ownership, and financial concerns, limiting our comprehension of the human body. One possible remedy involves developing a model capable of generating artificial images of the human form, tailored to specific characteristics like age, sex, and medical condition. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have allowed the creation of realistic 2D images of landscapes, but producing high-definition, 3D images of the human brain, accurate in form and realistic in quality, has been hindered by data scarcity and technological limitations. This project introduces a model capable of producing anatomically accurate, high-resolution, and realistic images of the human brain, allowing large-scale studies of human form and pathology while preserving patient confidentiality. This model also accelerates research in areas like anomaly detection, data synthesis, and the application of AI in a fair and ethical manner. The project's code and pre-trained models are available at: https://github.com/AmigoLab/SynthAnatomy.

Remote laptop privacy breaches are becoming increasingly prevalent, primarily through the exploitation of malware to access webcams and microphones.  Currently, there are limited solutions to prevent microphone-related attacks, despite the existence of webcam protection measures. In an effort to address this issue, a new system called TickTock has been proposed to detect the status of laptop microphones. This system works by monitoring the electromagnetic signals emanating from the laptop's circuitry, which are only present when the microphone is active. By testing TickTock on a diverse range of laptops, researchers were able to successfully demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately identifying microphone status in the vast majority of cases.

We generalize the fixed point theorem of Krasnoselskii to include non-self mappings. Our novel approach simplifies the existing proof of Hillam's result, removing the requirement of a compact or bounded image. This allows us to extend the applicability of Hillam's result to self-mappings defined on the real numbers. Furthermore, we provide a new, concise proof of the global convergence of the Newton-Raphson method.

Recent research has revealed that the iron chalcogenides exhibit intrinsic topological superconductivity, making them a promising material for quantum computation, thanks to their distinctive electronic properties. Calculations and experiments, including high-resolution photoemission and scanning tunneling microscopy, have confirmed the presence of topologically nontrivial surface states in FeTe$_{0.5}$Se$_{0.5}$. Yet, the evidence of topological surface states from electrical transport measurements was lacking. Conducting electrical transport experiments, we detected a topological transition characterized by a nonlinear Hall effect and a linear magnetoresistance near the superconducting critical temperature. Moreover, a sign change in the Hall coefficient, coupled with the concurrent softening of the ${A}_{1g}$ phonon mode at around 40 K, points to a nematic transition. This phenomenon, driven by the interaction between phonons and spins, highlights the presence of a highly fluctuating state. Our findings provide conclusive evidence of the topological surface states in FeTe$_{0.5}$Se$_{0.5}$ and shed new light on the underlying mechanism of superconductivity in the iron chalcogenide class.

The performance of two-dimensional quantum emitter arrays in the linear regime is explored for their role as efficient optical components. By analyzing the optical behavior of emitter pairs, we demonstrate the capability to manipulate the array's optical properties, including its transmission, resonance frequency, and spectral range. Our theoretical model, combined with numerical simulations, allows us to design and describe the array's behavior in response to fully polarized light, including the application of linear and circular polarizers, and phase shifters. This research highlights the significance of optimizing the array's geometric arrangement and the precise adjustment of external magnetic fields to achieve optimal performance.

One of the biggest scientific hurdles of our era revolves around comprehending the intricacies of SARS-CoV-2 evolution and transmission. By combining cutting-edge technologies like artificial intelligence, genomic data, extensive mutational analysis, and advanced computational tools, researchers discovered that the evolution of SARS-CoV-2 is largely controlled by a natural selection process based on the virus's infectivity. Two critical mutations, specifically at the L452 and N501 sites of the spike protein receptor-binding domain, were accurately predicted months before they emerged in dominant variants like Alpha, Delta, and Omicron. Subsequent studies also identified a new mechanism of natural selection: the development of antibodies resistant to the virus. The AI-driven forecasting of Omicron's contagiousness, vaccine effectiveness, and antibody resistance was later validated by experimental findings. Moreover, the model accurately predicted the replacement of the dominant BA.1 variant by BA.2 in March, and later correctly forecasted the emergence of Omicron variants BA.4 and BA.5 in June. Topological AI models have also proven to be effective in accurately predicting the impact of mutations on the efficacy of monoclonal antibodies.

In classical mechanics, specific position and momentum variables are chosen to facilitate the promotion of corresponding quantum operators, utilizing a particular set of coordinates. It's crucial to select a distinct set of variables, rather than a broad range, to ensure the validity of the quantization process. The chosen variables and their associated quantum operators are key to confirming a quantization's validity, as incorrect interpretations can lead to misguided physical conclusions. This analysis also covers particles, fields, and gravity.

One of the primary objectives in searching for continuous gravitational waves from neutron stars is to study the non-axisymmetric deformations of their crust. The maximum possible ellipticity resulting from the crust's deformation, also known as the "mountains," serves as a crucial upper limit in determining the strength of these gravitational wave sources. By employing the Gittins et al 2021 framework and a transverse force, we calculated a maximum ellipticity of 7.4 x 10^-6, which surpasses the initial findings of Gittins et al 2021, yet aligns with the earlier predictions by Ushomirsky et al 2000, indicating neutron stars could be substantial sources of continuous gravitational waves.

Modern deep learning model developers and owners are increasingly faced with the challenge of safeguarding their crowd-sourced, sensitive data against stringent privacy regulations. The primary technique currently employed to achieve privacy assurances relies on differential privacy, a method bolstered by optimization techniques. Although proven effective in fending off various types of attacks, differential privacy's efficacy comes at the cost of diminished model performance. This study investigates the DP-SGD algorithm, a differentially-private stochastic gradient descent technique, in contrast to standard optimization practices, including regularization methods. The analysis evaluates the resulting models' utility, training efficiency, and susceptibility to membership inference and model inversion attacks. Furthermore, the study delves into the limitations of differential privacy and experimentally verifies the superior privacy-preserving attributes of dropout and l2-regularization.

A new optomechanical inertial sensor, suitable for low-frequency measurements, has been developed. It features a resonant frequency of 4.7 Hz, a high mechanical quality factor, a small 2.6-gram test mass, and a projected noise floor of 5E-11 m s-2 per root-Hz at 1 Hz. This sensor's compact design, low power consumption, and resistance to external influences, including magnetic fields and air resistance, make it a promising choice for future geodesy missions. The paper showcases the sensor's performance in detecting low-frequency seismic noise by comparing it to a commercial seismometer, along with data analysis techniques to identify, characterize, and correct various noise sources.

Given two sequences of positive real numbers, $\{ a_{n}\}$ and $\{ b_{n}\}$, where $\{ a_{n}\}$ converges to positive infinity and $\{ b_{n}\}$ follows the asymptotic relationship $b_n\approx k\cdot a_{n}$, where $k$ is a positive constant, the limit of the expression $\left(1+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right)^{b_{n}}$ as $n$ approaches infinity equals $e^{k}$.

To ensure the reliability of object detection neural networks in high-stakes environments like autonomous vehicles or robotics, it's essential to test their robustness against unexpected hardware failures, including soft errors that can compromise a system's perception module. Standard metrics, based on average precision, provide a misleading assessment of model vulnerability by focusing on object-level rather than image-level impacts. This approach can result in an over- or underestimation of the safety risks associated with silent data corruption caused by memory bit flips. In response, we propose the Image-wise Vulnerability Metric for Object Detection (IVMOD) to evaluate the safety-related implications of faulty object detection due to incorrect image analysis, including the severity of false positives and negatives. Our evaluation of various object detection models reveals the severe consequences of hardware faults, including the generation of hundreds of false positives or the loss of up to 90% of true positives in a single image. Furthermore, a single stuck-at-1 fault can cause temporally persistent ghost detections, covering up to 83% of the image, while also leading to the continuous missed detection of actual objects, with up to 64% of true positives lost.

The classification accuracy of Hyperspectral Imaging (HSI) can significantly improve through Deep Learning, yet, the data sets are relatively small, and the learning process is not straightforward due to the high dimensionality of the data and the incompatibility of cameras from different manufacturers. To address these challenges, a novel approach incorporates a tailored model bias and adjusts the data dimension, employing a 2D convolutional model optimized for HSI. The proposed method outperforms traditional models in various applications, including inline inspection and remote sensing, and provides enhanced explanatory power, allowing the data-driven learning of camera filters, which can inform the design of an ideal camera.

Research has demonstrated that any perceived potential can theoretically be produced through quantum mechanics by utilizing a specific wavefunction. In our study, we focus on the particular example of the gravitational pull a test particle experiences across a range from planetary to cosmological scales, and we derive the wavefunction required to yield this gravitational potential. In essence, the observed gravitational interactions at various length scales can be attributed to an underlying wavefunction. The consequences of our findings are discussed.

The atomic energy shifts caused by hadronic vacuum polarization in hydrogen-like ions and muonic hydrogen are assessed through a semi-empirical approach.  An empirical hadronic polarization function, based on the experimental data of electron-positron annihilations into hadrons, is used to formulate a relativistic Uehling potential. Calculations of the hadronic vacuum polarization effects are performed for the low-lying levels, utilizing both the Dirac-Coulomb wave functions and the bound wave functions, which consider the finite nuclear size. Formulas are derived for the hadronic Uehling potential of a nucleus with a finite size, as well as the relativistic energy shifts in the case of a point-like nucleus. These findings are compared to the existing analytic formulas from the non-relativistic theory.

The CP asymmetry in the decay of a D0 meson into a K- and a K+ particle, a process suppressed by the Cabibbo mechanism, was measured using data from proton-proton collisions. The data, collected at a center of mass energy of 13 TeV, were obtained with the LHCb detector. The study required the D0 mesons to originate from the prompt decay of a D*+ meson, and the charge of the accompanying pion was used to determine the charm meson's initial state. The measured CP asymmetry in the decay of a D0 meson into a K- and a K+ particle was 6.8 times 10^-4, with a statistical uncertainty of 5.4 times 10^-4 and a systematic uncertainty of 1.6 times 10^-4. The direct CP asymmetries in the decays of a D0 meson into a K- and a K+ particle and a π- and a π+ particle were calculated by combining the measured CP asymmetry with the difference in CP asymmetry between the two decays. The calculated direct CP asymmetries were 7.7 times 10^-4 and 23.2 times 10^-4, respectively. The results indicate a high likelihood of direct CP violation in the decay of a D0 meson into a π- and a π+ particle, and the study provides the first evidence of direct CP violation in a specific D0 decay.

The decidability of the first-order logical theory of binary overlap-free words, and more broadly, of ${\alpha}$-free words for rational ${\alpha}$, where $2 < {\alpha} \leq 7/3$, has been established. This achievement enables the automated verification of previously laborious results regarding this class, leveraging a decision-making process.

The Swapped Dragonfly, denoted as D3(K;M) [1], features a structure of K global ports per router and M routers per group, resulting in a total of n=KMM routers. It represents a partially populated version of the Dragonfly. This study investigates the Swapped Dragonfly with restricted K and M, encompassing four distinct scenarios. Matrix multiplication: when K is a perfect square, a matrix product of size n can be achieved in sqrt(n) rounds. All-to-all data exchange: when K and M share a common factor s, the exchange operation can be performed in n/s rounds. Broadcast: the inclusion of a synchronized source-vector header enables the network to broadcast data in 3x/M rounds. Ascend-descend algorithm: when K and M are powers of 2, the algorithm's cost is comparable to that of a Boolean hypercube of the same size. Notably, the algorithms designed for the Swapped Dragonfly are free of link conflicts and are compared to those operating on a hypercube and a fully populated Dragonfly. Due to its versatile nature, the results obtained from the Swapped Dragonfly are more generalizable, as it contains emulations of various networks with restricted K and/or M.

The behavior of Activated Random Walks on finite networks, characterized by particles randomly entering and leaving at the boundary, has been thoroughly examined. In the absence of a known stationary distribution, the process's relaxation time was explicitly determined. Additionally, the equivalence of the separation cutoff to the product condition was demonstrated. Furthermore, the center and width of the cutoff window were precisely estimated. The results were applied to a range of networks, including: (i) finite subgraphs of infinite, non-amenable graphs, and (ii) finite, vertex-transitive graphs. Notably, the latter finding resolves a long-standing conjecture by Levine and Liang. The underlying proof leverages a refined analysis of a recently discovered stationary time, linked to the IDLA process.

The supersymmetry breaking mechanism typically forecasts the existence of sgoldstinos, which may function as wave-like dark matter particles. However, due to the widespread interaction with electromagnetic fields, the light scalar sgoldstino dark matter could result in variations of the fine-structure constant. Using precise atomic clock data, we are able to test the supersymmetry breaking scale $\sqrt{F}$ up to the GUT scale, provided the sgoldstino mass falls within the range of $4\times10^{-7}$ eV to $10^{-22}$ eV.

A novel formulation has been devised to calculate the tunneling action in vacuum decay, utilizing the concept of the tunneling potential. The newly formulated action was initially derived by ensuring that its variations yield the correct equations of motion and the same action value as the one computed from the Euclidean bounce. An alternative derivation of the tunneling potential action via canonical transformations is presented, encompassing single-field, multi-field, and gravitational scenarios. The potential applicability of the new approach to computing the functional determinant prefactor in the tunneling rate is also discussed.

The AWAKE CERN experiment sought to enhance the electron bunch's performance-critical stability and brightness at the proton-driven plasma wakefield. To achieve this, researchers implemented unsupervised machine learning approaches, testing numerical optimizers and model-free reinforcement learning agents. To prevent bias, reinforcement learning agents were trained using state encodings from auto-encoders. A synthetic model of the beamline was constructed to aid in hyper-parameter selection, utilizing a variational auto-encoder. This work presents novel methods combining deep learning and reinforcement learning to automate low-energy beamline setup, particularly at the AWAKE facility. Results from the applied machine learning techniques, including computer vision, are discussed, along with the potential for operational deployment and broader applicability.

The income from a player in freemium games originates from in-app purchases and advertisements they are exposed to. Players' game length impacts the likelihood of generating revenue, making early churn detection crucial. Identifying imminent player departure enables game retention strategies, increasing the player's game duration. This article explores enhanced churn prediction through the integration of sequential and aggregate data via diverse neural network configurations. Our analysis demonstrates that combining these data types surpasses models reliant solely on sequential or aggregate data, yielding superior prediction accuracy.

The astronomical field significantly benefits from understanding the Point Spread Function (PSF) of a specific instrument. We present a novel PSF Reconstruction algorithm designed for the LBT LUCI instrument, leveraging the SOUL SCAO module. Our method relies solely on synchronized wavefront sensor data and a limited set of calibration information. Unlike other approaches, we calculate a sequence of wavefront maps, each paired with a corresponding instantaneous PSF. To validate the algorithm, we conducted experiments in a controlled laboratory environment and in nighttime conditions, adapting the SOUL configurations to varying guide star magnitudes and atmospheric seeing. This technique, dubbed "BRUTE" (Blind Reconstruction Using TElemetry), employs a one-to-one mapping, translating each wavefront slope into a distinct instantaneous PSF.

A significant challenge in fundamental physics arises from the observation of a small, non-zero cosmological constant, contradicting theoretical predictions from quantum field theory by a factor of up to 10$^{120}$. The resolution of this enormous disparity between theory and observation is expected to be a feature of a complete quantum gravity theory. In our work, we examine the capacity of generalized uncertainty principle models, derived from phenomenological considerations, to tackle the cosmological constant problem. Specifically, we investigate how these models modify the phase space of quantum field theory, and the impact of this modification on the integration of zero-point energies in momentum space. Our analysis reveals several limitations of GUP models in their current form, making it unlikely they will effectively address the cosmological constant issue.

The interaction between the dark U(1) sector and the visible Standard Model sector occurs through the kinetic mixing of the dark photon U(1) field and the SM U(1)Y gauge field. After the electroweak and U(1)d symmetry breaking, the dark photon acquires mass and mixes with the SM neutral vector boson, resulting in a parity-violating coupling. This interaction can be studied in low-energy phenomenology and high-energy collider experiments. Future high-energy colliders, such as the proposed Large Hadron-electron collider, would allow for a detailed analysis of the dark photon's interaction with SM fermions, particularly through the polarization of lepton decay. By analyzing the strength of various variables in charge- and neutral-current processes, a $\chi^2$ analysis was performed, yielding 90% confidence level contours in the $\epsilon$-$m_{Z_d}$ and $\epsilon$-$g_V$ planes. These contours were used to impose limits on the dark photon mass, coupling strength, and Lorentz structure at a center-of-mass energy of approximately 1.3 TeV.

A new, innovative audio-visual speech enhancement solution, called MBURST, has been developed, taking into account the latest neurological findings on the brain, specifically the pyramidal cells in the prefrontal cortex. This groundbreaking approach, known as burst propagation, addresses the complex credit assignment problem in a more biologically authentic way by controlling the direction and intensity of plasticity through feedback, combining feedforward and feedback information, and simplifying complex connections. Leveraging these capabilities, MBURST identifies connections between the noisy audio and visual cues, thereby assigning significance to the speech by highlighting important information and minimizing noise. Experimental results, based on the Grid Corpus and CHiME3 dataset, demonstrate that MBURST produces comparable mask reconstructions to a baseline method, but with significantly improved energy efficiency, reducing neuron firing rates by up to 70% - a feature that promotes more sustainable implementations, making it suitable and beneficial for use in hearing aids and other embedded devices.

Autonomous vehicles are more likely to face severe weather conditions, making public safety a priority, especially as climate change increases the frequency of intense snowstorms. Current literature aims to enhance navigation capabilities in winter environments, but there's a lack of standard measures to quantify lidar sensor visibility reduction caused by precipitation. This chapter proposes a new metric to evaluate lidar visibility loss in real-time, drawing from the concept of visibility in meteorology. We test this metric on the Canadian Adverse Driving Conditions dataset, correlate it with a leading lidar-based localization algorithm, and analyze the benefits of filtering point clouds before the localization process. Our results show that the Iterative Closest Point algorithm exhibits unexpected robustness in snowy conditions, but abrupt weather events, such as intense snow gusts, significantly impair its accuracy.

The area of a black hole's event horizon is assumed to be a discrete, fermionic quantity, with a fixed relationship to the Planck length, and a finite, countable number of associated states. In investigating the entropy of a black hole, our primary focus lies in the phenomenon of self-similarity. By identifying a one-to-two correspondence between the states of the black hole and the partitioning of the integer N, we are able to develop a compositional framework that accounts for the configuration space of the black hole. Through this framework, we reveal the self-similarity of the black hole to stem from the inherent self-similarity of the partitioning of N. Furthermore, our findings are contrasted with the existing results regarding the quantum corrections to the entropy, which are shown to necessitate distinct statistical weights for the various states.

The MICADO instrument, a crucial component of the ESO ELT, offers cutting-edge imaging and spectroscopy capabilities at near-infrared wavelengths. The PSF Reconstruction Team at MICADO is pioneering a revolutionary software service, the first of its kind at ESO telescopes, to reconstruct the Point Spread Function (PSF) without the need for actual science data. This groundbreaking tool utilizes adaptive optics telemetry data from Single Conjugate and Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics modes, facilitated by the MORFEO module. The PSF-R service will play a pivotal role in the advanced post-processing analysis of MICADO's imaging and spectroscopic data. In this context, we present the current status of the PSF-R service, following the successful completion of the Final Design Review, and showcase recent findings from simulated and real-world data collected from instruments comparable to MICADO.

To decompose 3x3 matrices, we'll use commutators, obtaining polynomial identity satisfied decompositions, then apply these to infinite rank free module endomorphisms and bounded linear operators. Specifically, it has been shown that infinite-dimensional Hilbert space operators are the sum of four 3rd-order automorphisms, and simple rings from infinitely dimensional space endomorphism ring quotients are the sum of three nilpotent subrings.

The stabiliser group of a four-vector, or Wigner's little group, for massless particles, is determined as the largest solvable subgroup of the four-dimensional proper orthochronous Lorentz group, referred to as the Borel subgroup. In the absence of mass, massless particles are divided into left- and right-handed chiral states, controlled by the maximal solvable subgroups ${\rm sol}_2^\pm$ of order two. Subsequent Lorentz transformations are formulated and applied to the general representations of particle states. Moreover, the relationship between the spin-flip contribution and the occurrence of non-physical spin operators is demonstrated.

To achieve a balance between precision and soundness, researchers are working to improve the construction of static call graphs. Traditionally, program analysis techniques used to create these graphs are often imprecise. To overcome this, researchers have introduced a new method, employing machine learning to refine the call graphs built by static analysis. By extracting structural features from the graph, a random forest classifier removes edges identified as false positives. Despite these advances, the current approach still falls short, failing to account for the underlying source code meaning, and as a result, struggles to distinguish actual from non-actual calls. In response, a new technique, AutoPruner, has been proposed, utilizing a combination of statistical semantic and structural analysis to identify and remove false positives from the graph. By employing a transformer-based approach, AutoPruner captures the semantic relationships between the functions associated with each edge in the graph, achieved by fine-tuning a pre-trained code model. The semantic features are then used in conjunction with the graph's structural features to classify the edges via a neural network. Evaluations conducted on a dataset of real-world programs demonstrate that AutoPruner surpasses current benchmarks, yielding a 13% increase in the F-measure when identifying non-actual edges in a static call graph.

This work aims to analyze the underlying structure of the sandpile group in a specific set of self-replicating graphs. Specifically, we focus on the Abelian sandpiles present in Sierpinski gasket graphs, providing a clear definition of the identity element under standard boundary conditions. Furthermore, we derive a recursive formula to describe the sandpile group. In addition, our research explores the convergence rates of Abelian sandpile Markov chains on these graphs, offering enhanced bounds on the speed of convergence to a stationary state.

This paper explores the use of local projections in high-dimensional settings to estimate impulse responses. To achieve this, we employ the desparsified lasso method, which enables the estimation of high-dimensional local projections without imposing penalties on the parameter of interest. We then demonstrate the asymptotic normality of our proposed estimator under a broad set of conditions. Furthermore, our approach is validated through a simulation-based evaluation and applied to two prominent examples in the field of macroeconomic research, focusing on the effects of monetary policy and government spending.

Real-time object detection on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) presents a difficult problem due to the constrained processing capabilities of edge GPU devices used in Internet of Things (IoT) settings. To address this issue, a new, compact deep learning architecture named FasterX, built upon the YOLOX model, has been proposed for real-time object detection on edge GPU. Initially, a more efficient and compact PixSF head has been designed to replace the original YOLOX head, resulting in improved detection of small objects. By incorporating the depthwise separable convolution, the head becomes even more lightweight. Additionally, a slimmer structure, termed as SlimFPN, has been created in the Neck layer to reduce the network's parameters, striking a balance between accuracy and speed. Moreover, an attention module has been embedded in the Head layer to enhance the feature extraction capabilities of the prediction head. Furthermore, the label assignment strategy and loss function have been optimized to mitigate the issues of category imbalance and box optimization in UAV datasets. To improve the ability of the PixSF head in position embedding and feature extraction, auxiliary heads are presented for online knowledge distillation. The proposed FasterX models were validated through experiments on NVIDIA Jetson NX and Jetson Nano embedded platforms, achieving a superior trade-off between accuracy and latency compared to state-of-the-art models when tested on the VisDrone2021 dataset.

High-quality, ground-based observations with optimal resolution are currently attainable through cutting-edge adaptive optics technology, boasting high Strehl ratios. Nonetheless, the full scientific potential of these observations remains unrealized without a detailed understanding of the point spread function. For the next generation of 30-meter class telescopes, precise PSF characterization will be essential to meet the stipulated scientific objectives. In response, there is a growing demand for the development of reliable PSF reconstruction tools. In the context of the MICADO@ELT instrument, a planned service, our research team is tasked with developing a PSF reconstruction service. For MICADO, a blind approach to PSF reconstruction is being pursued, ensuring the greatest possible applicability across various science cases. This approach involves reconstructing the PSF without leveraging information from science data, relying instead on telemetry and calibration data. While our PSF reconstruction algorithm remains under development, its current implementation has reached a level of maturity that permits the testing of its performance with real observations. In the following presentation, the accuracy of our reconstructed PSFs and the resulting uncertainties in the measurement of scientific parameters for bright, on-axis observations obtained with the SOUL+LUCI instrument at the LBT will be discussed. This marks the first application of our algorithm to actual data, effectively demonstrating its readiness level and clearing the path for further testing. Our PSF reconstruction algorithm has proven capable of accurately reconstructing the Strehl ratio and full-width at half maximum of observed PSFs, boasting errors of less than 2% and 4.5%, respectively. To evaluate the scientific efficacy of the obtained reconstructed PSFs, a dedicated set of simulated observations of a paradigmatic science case was created.

Numerous independent sparse linear systems are encountered in various fields, such as plasma physics, astrophysics, and chemistry. These systems can be combined into a single large linear system, but doing so neglects the inherent structure of the systems, resulting in suboptimal performance. In contrast, modern accelerators are designed to handle multiple independent calculations efficiently. By solving each system independently, the optimal performance of Krylov solvers can be maintained, significantly reducing the need for kernel launches and global communication. To facilitate this approach, portable solvers are being developed to perform entire linear system solves within a single kernel launch.

The redshift space anisotropy of the bispectrum in galaxy surveys is typically characterized by multipole moments, whose detectability depends on the level of statistical fluctuations. We develop a method to calculate these fluctuations in the context of a galaxy survey similar to the Euclid mission. We analyze the detectability of bispectrum multipoles in such a survey, focusing on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and the correlation between measurement errors. Based on our findings, the Euclid mission should be able to measure bispectrum multipoles up to a certain order, depending on the scale and redshift of the observed triangles formed by the k-vectors in Fourier space. While the highest order multipoles are difficult to detect, the lower order multipoles are detectable even at large scales, allowing for the combination of measurements to increase the effective signal-to-noise ratio.

This research examines the application of Reinforcement Learning in partially observable systems, focusing on the Predictive State Representations (PSR) model, a comprehensive framework encompassing other notable models such as Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes. PSR uses a set of predictions to represent states, relying solely on observable information. We introduce a new, model-based algorithm that enables the PSR to learn an almost optimal policy, with a sample complexity that grows polynomially in relation to the system's parameters. Our method naturally accommodates function approximation, allowing it to handle systems with large state and observation spaces. We demonstrate that, given a realistic model class, the algorithm's sample complexity grows polynomially with the model class's statistical complexity, independent of the state and observation spaces' sizes. Notably, our work achieves a new milestone by demonstrating that polynomial sample complexities can match the globally optimal policy in PSR. Furthermore, our theorem provides a foundation for establishing sample complexity bounds in specific models, including m-step weakly revealing and m-step decodable tabular POMDPs, as well as POMDPs with low-rank latent transitions and linear emissions.

Matrix multiplication approximations that don't sacrifice too much accuracy could greatly lower the cost of neural network predictions. By replacing expensive calculations with quicker table-lookups, recent research used a fast hash function generated from training data. In this study, we refine previous work, focusing on the neural network prediction context, where both training data and pre-learned model weights are available. We suggest a fine-tuning method to accelerate entire neural networks with a minimal drop in precision. Our method is then tested on a basic image classification task. Although our method shows improvements over previous work, the overall classification accuracy remains noticeably lower than the exact matrix multiplication. Despite the negative outcome, our study paves the way for future research to develop fast non-linear hashing methods that speed up inner product calculations.

Explicit calculations of Vafa-Witten invariants are conducted for 3-dimensional manifolds, mirroring the Floer groups in the context of Donaldson theory. Specifically, the invariants are computed in a set of illustrative examples, such as the Gluck twist, knot surgeries, and log-transforms, which are related to various surgery operations. Moreover, the structural characteristics anticipated to hold for 3-manifolds in general are outlined, including the action of the modular group, the connection to Floer homology, the infinite-dimensionality of the invariants, and the non-existence of instantons.

Higgs bosons consisting of doublets, a common occurrence in Standard Model extensions, are prominent targets in collider searches, such as the Large Hadron Collider, due to the potential presence of new, heavy Higgs bosons. In such scenarios, the presence of heavy Higgs bosons restricts the possible decay modes, primarily favoring fermionic channels, although bosonic modes may produce cleaner signals. However, when the Higgs sector includes additional singlet states, the situation becomes more complex, with the possibility of Higgs-to-Higgs decays dominating. To accurately interpret the experimental data, the impact of radiative corrections must be taken into account. In this study, the bosonic decays of heavy doublet-dominated Higgs bosons in the MSSM and NMSSM are examined at full one-loop order, considering the implications of the SU(2) symmetry and the emergence of non-resonant contributions to boson final states.

This study shows that discontinuous shear thickening can occur even in a
thin or relatively dense suspension of non-frictional soft particles. We find
that discontinuous shear thickening represents a rapid, transient transition
in inertial suspensions. Our theoretical model, developed using a simplified
approach, accurately matches the simulation outcomes across a broad range of
volume fractions, without the need for any specific adjustments.

Sustainable development goals and global climate targets heavily rely on the functionality of dam reservoirs, but a lack of consistent data regarding the geographical location of these dams, particularly the smaller ones, poses a significant challenge. To bridge this data gap, a novel method involves the use of globally accessible remote sensing imagery to perform automated extraction of dam reservoirs. This task can be seen as a finer-grained sub-task of water body extraction, requiring the extraction of water areas from images and the subsequent separation of dam reservoirs from natural water bodies. We suggest a novel deep neural network-based framework, dividing the extraction of dam reservoirs into two distinct steps: the segmentation of water bodies from the background, followed by the classification of these water bodies as either dam reservoirs or natural water bodies. In the segmentation phase, point-level metric learning across images addresses the ambiguity between water areas and land regions, while in the classification phase, prior-guided metric learning from clusters optimizes the image embedding space at a finer level, taking into account clusters of reservoirs. To foster further research, a benchmark dataset comprising earth imagery and human-labelled reservoirs from river basins in West Africa and India has been established. Our method has been extensively tested on this benchmark in the tasks of water body segmentation, dam reservoir recognition, and joint dam reservoir extraction, resulting in superior performance when compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

The presence of localized residual stress and elastic strain concentrations in microelectronic devices, such as those found in HEMTs, has a profound impact on device performance, resistance to thermal damage, and radiation resistance. Characterizing these concentrations, however, poses a significant challenge due to their tiny dimensions, requiring novel, non-invasive methods. In this study, we employed synchrotron X-ray differential aperture X-ray microscopy to map strain concentrations within a gallium nitride layer in HEMTs at a sub-micron level. Our analysis revealed significant changes in the strain fields between pristine and irradiated HEMT specimens, including a notable reduction in lattice plane spacing in the gallium nitride following gamma-irradiation, attributed to radiation-induced damage.

Ensuring the reliability of software AI-based medical devices under real-world conditions prior to clinical use is essential for evaluating safety, efficiency, and usability. Given the complexity of developing large labeled medical datasets and the stringent regulations governing medical device software, we propose a method to predict the performance of an unknown, unaltered AI model on a new, unlabeled data set. Our proposed method, based on conformal prediction, assesses the accuracy of the model without modifying the training process or relying on assumptions about the original data. We test our method on three diverse medical imaging datasets, simulating real-world scenarios, and hope that our work will facilitate the development of standardized, effective evaluation methods, ultimately leading to more robust and trustworthy clinical AI tools.

A forward modeling framework has been developed to estimate the distribution of galaxy redshifts from photometric surveys. The framework includes a detailed population model, a stellar population synthesis model, a data-model characterizing the observation process, and an explicit treatment of selection cuts. This method offers advantages, including not relying on spectroscopic calibration data, explicit control over modeling assumptions, and a direct link between photo-$z$ inference and galaxy evolution physics. In addition to estimating redshift distributions, forward modeling enables the drawing of robust inferences about the statistical properties of the galaxy population. We demonstrate the effectiveness of forward modeling by estimating the redshift distributions of the GAMA and VVDS surveys, comparing the results to their spectroscopic redshifts. Our baseline model accurately predicts the tomographic redshift distributions for GAMA and VVDS with a small bias, indicating its potential to meet the accuracy requirements of Stage III cosmological surveys. We expect further improvements to forward modeling, including hyper-parameter fitting, to enable accurate redshift distribution inference for Stage IV surveys.

A new, analytically solvable model of a bipedal robot has been developed, allowing it to walk on uneven surfaces and inclines. The robot's walking pattern arises from the interaction between a stationary leg in a pendulum-like motion and a trailing leg with articulated motion. Gaiting becomes possible due to the interplay between the stationary and trailing legs, the energy-conserving pendulum motion, and the switching of leg roles. The robot's adaptability to uneven surfaces and inclines relies on the constant maximal angle between the legs during stride transitions and the adjustable duration of each stride. This model offers a closed-form solution, allowing the simulation of different bipedal motions in both forward and reverse directions. Moreover, the speed of the robot's gait has been optimised with respect to its design parameters.

This research investigates the influence of insoluble surfactants on the spatio-temporal development of turbulent jets. We utilized a 3D numerical simulation method, accounting for the effects of surfactant-induced Marangoni stresses. Our study builds upon previous work examining the interaction between vortices and surfaces in the absence of surfactants. We obtained numerical solutions across a broad spectrum of Weber and elasticity numbers, considering both surface deformation and Marangoni stresses as sources of vorticity. Our findings highlight the significant role of Marangoni stresses, driven by surfactant concentration gradients, in the creation of coherent, hairpin-like vortex structures. These structures play a critical role in shaping the 3D interfacial dynamics. Furthermore, we derived theoretical expressions describing the rate of circulation production in the presence of surfactants, a general 3D two-phase flow, and demonstrated the prominent influence of Marangoni stresses.

To study the influence of radiation pressure during the formation of a 
globular cluster, researchers conducted a simulation of a collision between 
two massive, turbulent gas clouds. Using a series of hypothetical models, 
they explored how the absence or presence of starlight or supernovae 
influenced the development of a star cluster. They found that a tightly 
bound star cluster, consisting of around 100,000 stars, emerged within 3 
million years when two gas clouds, each containing 360,000 stars, collided. 
This cluster did not arise from a single collapsing event but from the 
merging of small, dense gas clumps, along with the gradual accumulation 
of additional gas. The cluster's growth was primarily impeded by the 
momentum transferred from the absorption of starlight, with photoionization 
becoming significant only after a sufficient number of stars had formed. 
Comparing the simulations, the absence of radiation pressure resulted in a 
star cluster twice as massive, with the effect being even more pronounced 
(16%) when considering the influence of Lyman-alpha radiation. In the 
simulations accounting for radiation pressure, supernovae occurred after the 
star-forming gas had been dispersed, meaning the metals expelled by these 
explosions were not immediately reused to create new stars.

On considère une variété projective lisse définie sur un corps de nombres. En supposant que la cohomologie à 2-étoiles $\ H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)$ soit nulle, des résultats précédents ont prouvé que le sous-groupe de torsion du groupe de Chow en codimension 2, noté $CH^2(X)_{tors}$, est fini. Dans cette note, nous obtenons des bornes uniformes pour le groupe fini $CH^2(X)_{tors}$, qui varie en famille. Let a smooth projective variety over a number field be considered. Under the assumption that the 2-nd cohomology group H^2(X, O_X) = 0, prior results showed that the torsion subgroup of the 2-nd codimension Chow group, denoted as CH^2(X)_{tors}, is finite. In this note, uniform bounds are given for the finite group CH^2(X)_{tors}, when the variety varies in a family.

Quasiparticle excitations play a significant part in the functioning of superconducting quantum systems, including qubits and sensors. In this research, the behavior of these excitations in specific weak links with several subgap states is investigated. We demonstrate that nearly complete dynamic polarization within a given parity category can be achieved by applying a microwave pulse synchronized with a transition in the opposing parity category. Our theoretical findings are supported by recent experiments involving hybrid semiconductor nanowire Josephson junctions, providing valuable insights for efficiently manipulating the parity state of Andreev-based qubits.

This paper builds upon existing knowledge of generalized solitons, known as $q$-solitons, by broadening the scope to include non-compact cases.  We achieve this by imposing specific regularity constraints on the vector field $X$ and curvature requirements on the manifold $M$.  Utilizing the tensor $q$'s inherent properties, we find that these non-compact $q$-solitons are stable under a specific transformation and exhibit a flat profile.  Ultimately, we apply our general theorems to specific cases, including ambient obstruction solitons, Cotton solitons, and Bach solitons, to demonstrate the practicality of our findings.

Many binary star systems with exoplanets start out within a star-forming cluster, 
where the gravitational forces from other stars cause significant changes in the 
binary-planet system. We ran simulations of a specific type of planet, with masses 
and orbits similar to the solar system's 4 largest planets, orbiting around a smaller 
binary star. We modeled the binary-planet system along with its surrounding star 
cluster. In around 10% of the cases, the gravitational forces from the star cluster 
made the binary star's closest point to its companion pass near the planets, causing 
instability. Even when the initial orbits of the binary star were stable enough to 
allow the planets to survive, the gravitational forces from the star cluster could 
still cause the planets to collide with each other, resulting in the loss of smaller 
planets and increased eccentricity of the larger planets. In many cases, the 
planetary systems lost their binary companions before the star cluster broke apart, 
which could cause the remaining planets to appear as if they had always been 
orbiting a single star. Furthermore, the gravitational forces from the star cluster 
also caused the planets' axes to become misaligned with their orbits, a phenomenon 
where the planets' axes wobble around as the binary star exerts a gravitational 
influence. In cases with the highest degree of misalignment, the planets' axes 
typically retained the binary companion and the planets themselves.

Deep neural networks are capable of approximating a wide range of nonlinear functions, 
which can be explicitly defined or treated as a complex system. The first neural function 
approximator, the Deep Operator Network, was introduced in 2019 based on a theoretical 
framework. Following its introduction, several other, albeit less comprehensive, function 
approximators have been developed, including graph-based networks and Fourier-based 
models. While the training of these models relies solely on data when dealing with 
black-box systems, incorporating the underlying equations into the training process 
can enhance the accuracy of physics-informed models. Neural function approximators 
can be effectively used in a multitude of applications, including real-time inference, 
design problems, uncertainty quantification, and autonomous systems. Furthermore, 
pre-trained DeepONets can be easily integrated into complex systems, requiring only 
minimal additional training. In this review, we examine the DeepONet, the Fourier 
neural operator, and the graph neural operator, along with their respective extensions, 
and explore their utility in various fields, including computational mechanics, 
porous media, fluid mechanics, and solid mechanics.

Mental health and emotion-aware computing heavily rely on accurate emotion prediction. However, the multifaceted nature of emotion, influenced by a person's physical well-being, mental status, and surroundings, makes this task particularly demanding. We address this challenge by utilizing mobile sensing data to forecast an individual's emotional state, specifically happiness and stress. In addition to physiological factors, our approach incorporates environmental influences, including weather and social interactions. We utilize phone data to build social networks, design a machine learning framework that aggregates user information from the graph network, and synchronizes it with temporal data dynamics to predict user emotions. Notably, constructing social networks does not incur additional user data or survey costs, and raises minimal privacy concerns. We propose a scalable architecture that automates the integration of social networks with user emotion predictions, effectively addressing the dynamic nature of real-life social networks. Our thorough evaluation underscores the benefits of social network integration, while our subsequent investigation highlights the significance of graph topology in determining model performance.

We investigated the use of skeletonization to simplify the description of intricate liquid formations within a surrounding fluid, often generated by turbulent motions such as splashing or fragmentation. We employed a modified approach to skeletonize a periodically flowing liquid, adapting a method previously developed for coarse-graining multiphase flows. This process involves diffusing an index function, concurrently moving the interface, until the two converge, forming a skeleton. The resulting skeleton captures the fundamental structure of the liquid jet, and the amount of interface movement or volume accumulation during the process can be used to approximate the original jet. We evaluated various quantitative metrics to characterize and differentiate the resulting skeletons, including standard morphometric parameters, such as branch length distributions, and a more sophisticated Topology Morphology Descriptor (TMD), to provide a concise, topological representation of the skeleton structures.

The intricacies of Recommender Systems are largely a result of being integrated into larger applications, 
influencing user experiences through various interfaces. Consequently, 
existing research has primarily focused on the systems' ability to generate accurate rankings, 
leaving the evaluation of RS behavior in real-world settings underrepresented. 
This narrow focus has hindered RSs' ability to leave a lasting impression in the real world, 
making them susceptible to adverse effects, such as exacerbating data imbalances. 
To promote a discussion among practitioners and establish new, publicly accessible methodologies 
for assessing RSs' performance in real-world environments, we introduce the EvalRS challenge.

Human-object interactions are crucial for a complete understanding of visual scenes, with spatial relationships between humans and objects being key indicators of interactions. We introduce a graph-based approach called SGCN4HOI, utilizing a skeleton-aware graph convolutional network, to detect these interactions. By combining geometric, visual, and spatial features, the model captures the intricate relationships between human and object keypoints. Additionally, a new representation method, based on skeletons, enhances object structure retention and improves human-object interaction detection. Evaluations using the V-COCO dataset demonstrate that SGCN4HOI outperforms existing pose-based models and matches or surpasses other approaches.

Over the past few decades, Europe has faced numerous delays in expanding its electricity transmission infrastructure, despite its crucial role in integrating renewable energy sources. Establishing a hydrogen network utilizing the existing fossil gas infrastructure could address the growing demand for low-emission fuels, while also helping to stabilize renewable energy fluctuations across the continent, thereby reducing the need for power grid expansion. We investigate this concept by adjusting the expansion of electricity and hydrogen grids within a sector-integrated, zero-carbon energy system, with a focus on regions with high renewable energy shares. Covering 181 regions, with a focus on every third hour of a year, allows us to accurately capture bottlenecks in transmission, as well as the variability in renewable energy supply and demand. Our findings consistently highlight the benefits of a pan-continental hydrogen backbone, connecting regions with high renewable energy production, demand centers, synthetic fuel production, and geological storage facilities. Building a hydrogen network can decrease system costs by up to 6%, with the most significant benefits when reinforcing the electricity grid is not feasible. Furthermore, between 58% and 66% of the backbone could be constructed using repurposed natural gas pipelines. While a hydrogen network can only partially replace power grid expansion, combining both approaches can achieve the greatest cost savings, up to 12%.

We use observational data from the first three years of the Dark Energy Survey, 
combined with external information, to constrain various extensions to the 
standard Lambda-CDM model. We incorporate simulated and real data, analyzed
