blindly, to ensure the robustness of our results. Unfortunately, the 
constraining power of our analysis is often limited by the lack of reliable 
predictions for nonlinear effects at the required precision. We investigate 
five types of model extensions: time-dependent dark energy, spatial curvature, 
sterile neutrinos, modifications to gravitational physics, and a model of 
structure growth. Using only the Dark Energy Survey data, we find that the 
time-varying equation of state of dark energy has a pivot redshift of 0.24, 
yielding a 68% confidence interval of -0.99 to -0.17, or -1.03 with a 
standard error of 0.04, at a pivot redshift of 0.21 when all data are 
combined. We obtain constraints on spatial curvature and effective relativistic 
species from external data, finding a value of 0.0009 with a 1.7% error, 
and 3.1 with a 0.2% error, respectively. We set a new, three times tighter 
limit on the mass of massive sterile neutrinos, finding a 95% confidence 
limit of 0.20 eV. We also constrain two types of gravitational physics 
modifications, finding a 0.4% error in the first parameter, and a 0.2% 
error in the second parameter, when all data are combined. Our results 
indicate that there is no significant evidence for physics beyond the 
standard Lambda-CDM model.

Schmidt recently conducted a survey that revealed connections between generalized bent functions, group-invariant Butson Hadamard matrices, and abelian splitting relative difference sets. We expand upon this discovery by exploring the equivalences between Butson matrices that are related by a common structure, rather than being directly group invariant. This finding has various implications, including the construction of Boolean functions with generalized partially bent expansions, even in scenarios where traditional bent functions are not feasible.

Electron beams with extremely short lifespans, lasting from femtoseconds to picoseconds, 
provide a unique opportunity to delve into cutting-edge areas, encompassing the dynamic 
structure of molecules at an ultra-fast pace, as well as the impact of extremely high 
radiation rates on biological systems. We present a straightforward method to generate 
electron beams with energies in the MeV range, using a tightly focused, multi-millijoule 
infrared femtosecond laser, even in ambient air. At a distance of one meter from the 
source, the electron beam emits a radiation dose exceeding the yearly safety limit within 
just a second, necessitating immediate protective measures. Computer simulations, using 
particles, verify that the acceleration process relies on the relativistic force acting upon 
charged particles, and the results are consistent with the observed electron energies. 
Additionally, the feasibility of scaling up this approach with the advancement of 
high-average power lasers, while opening up new avenues for the application of FLASH 
radiation therapy.

Quantum speed limits set a minimum pace for the evolution of physical systems, 
establishing a lower boundary for the rate at which a system's quantum state or 
an observable can change. We expand upon this concept, creating a generalized 
quantum speed limit that applies to unitary operator flows, a fundamental 
component in both quantum and classical systems. We establish two types of 
speed limits, investigating the point at which they merge, using a qubit and a 
random matrix Hamiltonian as exemplary systems. Our findings are then applied 
to the dynamic behavior of autocorrelation functions, leading to measurable 
limits on the responsiveness of out-of-equilibrium quantum systems and the 
quantum Fisher information, a key factor in precision quantum parameter 
estimation.

A novel, three-dimensional reconfigurable robot has been introduced, featuring a modular design composed of interlocking cubes. These robots utilize an innovative actuation system, relying on electromagnets integrated into the cube edges. By selectively pairing identically or oppositely polarized electromagnets, the system generates repulsive or attractive forces, facilitating the creation of hinges and enabling pivotal movements. Through the combination of attraction and repulsion, the robot can undergo reconfiguration, with its constituent modules, referred to as Electrovoxels, being actuated via electromagnetic pivoting. Experimental validation has been achieved through the development of fully autonomous, three-dimensional robots, which successfully demonstrate 2D and 3D self-reconfiguration capabilities, both on a laboratory air-table and during microgravity conditions. Furthermore, the hardware design, pivoting framework, reconfiguration planning software, and system dynamics are discussed, providing essential insights for the creation of scalable, self-reconfigurable robots.

The main focus of this paper revolves around the issue of reconstructing a low-rank matrix from its partially observed and noisy components. Under specified conditions, a novel, noise-agnostic, square-root matrix completion estimator has been proven to achieve the best possible results in solving the noisy matrix completion problem. Like its counterpart, the square-root Lasso estimator, this new estimator operates independently of noise magnitude. Although the problem of solving the square-root matrix completion estimator translates into a convex program, its statistical analysis relies heavily on its close association with a non-convex rank-constrained estimator.

We investigate a linearized version of the Calderon problem, focusing on polyharmonic operators of order 2m, where m is 2 or greater, drawing inspiration from Calderon's pioneering work. Our analysis leads to a uniqueness theorem, demonstrating the potential to recover coefficients up to a specified order, 2m-1, with a guarantee of up to gauge, using the inverse of momentum ray transforms.

A warped protoplanetary disk creates an ideal environment for pressure traps to form. Overcoming the meter-sized hurdle during the initial stages of planetary development poses a significant challenge. Several theories exist to address this obstacle, with pressure traps being a potential solution, enabling the temporary halting of planetesimal movement. Despite its importance, the origins and characteristics of pressure traps remain poorly understood. As warped disks are common among accretion disks, particularly those associated with planetary formation, it's proposed that these distortions contribute to the formation of pressure traps, aiding in the bypassing of the meter-sized barrier. We investigate the pressure trap profiles generated by an external torque, exploring its implications on planetary development in diverse environments, such as circumbinary disks and gap edges.

Our analysis utilizes a conformal moment expansion to study the global properties of generalized parton distributions. By employing a universal moment parameterization, we are able to fit parton distribution functions from phenomenology, lattice-calculated form factors, and direct lattice GPDs from large-momentum effective theory. Specifically, this work focuses on the behavior of parton distribution functions as a function of momentum transfer, while the same strategy can be applied to other regions with additional parameters. We demonstrate the potential of this approach with a detailed analysis of quark properties in protons, including quark transverse momentum and spatial distribution.

A key concept, the d-separation criterion, checks if a joint probability distribution aligns with a directed acyclic graph by detecting specific conditional independences. Our research contributes to this area by developing a new understanding of causal models, a unique d-separation definition, and a generalized version of the d-separation criterion. These efforts offer two primary advantages. Firstly, the categorical d-separation is an accessible and clear criterion rooted in topological relationships. Secondly, the results are applicable across various frameworks, encompassing not only traditional probability theory but also deterministic and uncertain networks. Consequently, this work establishes a comprehensive proof demonstrating the equivalence between local and global Markov properties and causal compatibility across continuous, mixed, deterministic, and uncertain variables.

Research into the quantum properties of matter, particularly those involving strongly correlated electrons, has led to a significant interest in twisted multilayers of two-dimensional materials. These structures, featuring a twisted pattern caused by relative layer movement, create unique potential landscapes that lead to electron confinement. Although numerous 2D materials exist, the study of twisted layered structures has only just begun. We've developed a comprehensive, first-principle model to examine the electronic properties of twisted Janus transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers. Our model, accounting for lattice deformation, stacking-dependent mass, and spin-orbit interactions, has been applied to over a hundred material combinations. Our findings indicate that the unique properties of twisted bilayers depend on the materials' composition, stacking orientation, and twist angle, allowing the formation of distinctive electronic networks. Furthermore, the spin-orbit effects inherent to these systems can dominate the material's bandwidth at smaller twist angles. Our work enables a detailed investigation of twisted Janus structures, paving the way for the discovery and control of new electronic phenomena.

We examine the fundamental nature of the primordial curvature perturbation using observations of dark matter substructure. By assuming an increase in the curvature perturbation spectrum at wavenumbers greater than 1 megaparsec, we model the development of host halos and subhalos using semi-analytic methods, taking into account potential uncertainties in the subhalo growth due to tidal stripping. Our findings lead to a new, robust constraint on the curvature perturbation with an added component, using the number of dwarf spheroidal galaxies in the Milky Way and the observations of the stellar streams. We discover an upper limit of approximately 10^-7 for the amplitude of this component at a wavenumber of 10^3 megaparsecs, as well as a potential boost factor of up to 10^4, which could impact indirect dark matter detection.

A retinal trait, or phenotype, reduces a retinal image to a singular, quantitative value. Calculating this trait from an image, however, can be a laborious process due to the complexity of the images. As a result, researchers typically discard a significant portion of available data due to the need for high-quality images. We suggest an alternative, the Deep Approximation of Retinal Traits (DART), which utilizes a neural network to approximate the output of an established pipeline. By training the network on degraded images, DART achieves a robust, single-step process. We tested DART using retinal images from the UK Biobank, which demonstrated a strong agreement with the established pipeline, even when images were degraded. Notably, DART computes retinal fractal dimensions at a rate of over 1,000 images per second, making it a promising tool for retinal analysis.

Binary neutron star mergers will create a large amount of fast-moving material, 
with speeds up to 60% the speed of light. When this material interacts with the 
surrounding interstellar medium, it produces a significant amount of synchrotron 
radiation across the radio to X-ray spectrum. Analytical models that take into 
account the varying speeds and energies of the material, represented by a 
power-law distribution, are developed. These models, which accurately 
account for the gradual deceleration of the material, offer a significant 
improvement over previous estimates, which overestimated the observed 
radiation by an order of magnitude. As a result, scientists will be able to 
make more accurate inferences about the material ejected during a merger, 
such as GW170817, which could lead to the detection of detectable radio and 
X-ray signals over a period of approximately 10,000 days.

Research has discovered that icicles grown from contaminated water exhibit a distinct wavelike pattern, attributed to a morphological instability. By cultivating icicles with controlled amounts of impurities, it has been observed that a portion of the contaminants remain encapsulated within the icicle, resulting in distinct internal formations. These internal structures, comprising chevron patterns, are aligned with the icicle's ripples, while displaying a substructure of curved shapes. Furthermore, an investigation into the crystal structure of laboratory-grown icicles, with and without added impurities, has provided a comprehensive understanding of the growth patterns within icicles. This study sheds new light on the underlying causes of the ripples, offering significant insights into the stability mechanism.

The significance of casual, unplanned conversations in maintaining our overall well-being and the creation of advanced interactive social tools cannot be overstated. Existing studies that directly assess the quality of social interactions have narrowly defined it as reduced trivial talk. However, other research has approached the topic from a broader angle, examining aspects such as rapport or engagement, but only as isolated factors. This study bridges this gap by introducing a comprehensive framework for evaluating conversation quality, rooted in the collaborative aspects of cooperative interactions. By adopting a multi-faceted perspective, we developed and validated two tools to assess perceived conversation quality at both the individual and group levels. We aimed to capture external observers' overall impressions of participants' experiences from short, fragmented interactions, and collected PCQ annotations from a publicly available dataset of natural, in-the-wild conversations. Furthermore, we analyzed the behavioral characteristics that contribute to higher PCQ, finding that external raters tend to associate higher-quality conversations with smaller group sizes, equitable turn-taking with fewer interruptions, and synchronized physical movements with increased PCQ.

A new binary neural network-based model, BRILLsson, has been developed to handle a wide range of non-semantic speech tasks. By utilizing a distillation process from a large, real-valued model, BRILLsson can achieve comparable performance with significantly reduced size, reaching 2MB, and faster execution, below 8ms, making it suitable for deployment in resource-constrained devices. BRILLsson has been evaluated across eight speech-based benchmarks, showing that its ultra-compact, low-latency architecture can rival large-scale models.

Machine learning fairness researchers have converged on key fairness criteria, 
which offer precise definitions of what it means for an ML model to be fair. 
Despite their importance, these criteria are hindered by significant limitations. 
We pinpoint four critical shortcomings of these formal fairness criteria, 
and aim to rectify them by integrating a distributionally robust objective 
into performative prediction.

We investigate the possibility that early universe black holes, known as primordial black holes, contain an electric charge that has persisted up to the present day.  We determine that black holes initially form with a non-zero charge, sourced from fluctuations and charged particle collisions.  Although the sign of the charge could vary, it could be shielded from discharge due to magnetic fields from rotating black holes.  Additionally, charged, rotating black holes can generate magnetic fields capable of counteracting the effects that cause the black holes to emit or absorb charged particles.  As a result, black holes could maintain their charge over an extended period.  Ultimately, the plasma in the dark matter halos could impart a net negative charge to the black holes, yielding average charges of -10^-32 C/kg or -10^-22 C/kg, depending on the black hole mass.  Given that the black hole charges are below the threshold required to discharge, it is possible that black holes could remain slightly non-neutral.  This suggests that black holes could maintain a net charge, albeit significantly lower than the maximum possible, which could lead to the possibility that charged, stable black holes could compose all of the dark matter in the universe.

Capturing the detailed distribution of mass in large galaxies distorted by strong gravity has become increasingly complex. Advances in imaging technology provide high-resolution and depth, but simple models fail to accurately depict the varied scales, structures, and morphologies involved. To address this, a new multiscale approach utilizing wavelet analysis has been developed. We tested this approach using simulated Hubble Space Telescope images featuring various types of mass substructures, including a small, localized dark matter halo, a non-localized field of subhalos, and irregular, multipolar galaxy shapes. Our results demonstrate that wavelet analysis successfully recovers these complex structures. By incorporating gradient-informed optimization, automatic differentiation, and parameter sampling, this approach integrates analytical, pixelated, and machine-learning techniques into a unified framework. This methodology is well-suited for quickly analyzing large collections of lenses, and all related tools are now available in the Herculens package.

In this study, the qualitative effects of a non-constant shear viscosity to entropy density ratio, dependent on baryon chemical potential, are investigated in hydrodynamic simulations. Since previous research primarily focused on the temperature dependence or a constant viscosity, this work delves into the impact of a generalized viscosity-entropy ratio, which accounts for both temperature and baryon chemical potential. By parameterizing the viscosity-entropy ratio directly in energy density and net baryon number, the model reduces bias from the equation of state. This study examines the system size, energy, and observable dependencies, as well as the effect on the RHIC - BES region. It finds that the net baryon number dependence has a negligible effect on elliptic flow, except in the early stages, while serving as a viable proxy for viscosity in non-equilibrium transport.

Our research investigates the relationship between transverse momentum and the Sivers asymmetry in two processes, SIDIS and Drell-Yan, which involve a transversely polarized proton target. By examining the weighted asymmetry, which takes into account the transverse momentum, we can express it as a product of the transverse-moments of parton distribution functions and fragmentation functions. Using specific parameters, we calculated the weighted Sivers asymmetry in SIDIS and Drell-Yan processes, mimicking the kinematics of the COMPASS experiment, and compared the results with available experimental data. Our findings indicate that the calculated SIDIS weighted Sivers asymmetry aligns with recent COMPASS measurements. However, the Drell-Yan program's preliminary data has significant uncertainties, requiring high-precision experimental data to validate the sign change property of the Sivers function between SIDIS and Drell-Yan processes, as well as to refine the sea quark Sivers function.

Helium-3 has become a crucial subject in various fields, including fundamental physics, nuclear and atomic structure, magnetometry, metrology, chemistry, and medicine. Specifically, research has proposed the use of $^3$He nuclear magnetic resonance probes as a new standard for absolute magnetometry. To achieve this, an accurate value of the $^3$He nuclear magnetic moment is necessary. However, it has only been indirectly determined with a relative precision of 12 parts per billion. This study focuses on the $^3$He$^+$ ground-state hyperfine structure in a Penning trap to directly measure the nuclear $g$-factor, the zero-field hyperfine splitting, and the bound electron $g$-factor. The measurements provide a new, highly accurate value for the $^3$He$^+$ nuclear $g$-factor, which enables the determination of the $g$-factor of the bare nucleus. This achievement allows for the first direct calibration of $^3$He NMR probes, representing an improvement of one order of magnitude over previous indirect results. Additionally, the study provides a two-order-of-magnitude improvement in the precision of the zero-field hyperfine splitting, allowing the determination of the Zemach radius.

A type of survival model known as the accelerated failure time model, or AFT, uses a logarithmic relationship to connect the time it takes for an event to occur with various factors. Unlike other models, the impact of these factors directly affects the time it takes, resulting in an interpretation that is easier to understand. This model, which doesn't specify the distribution of errors, has a number of beneficial properties, including its ability to withstand deviations from the expected distribution. Due to its desirable characteristics, it has emerged as a promising substitute for the Cox model in the analysis of censored time data. However, research has shown that the model typically uses a linear predictor, which doesn't account for non-linearity. Researchers have recently become increasingly interested in deep neural networks, which have achieved remarkable success in a range of fields. By leveraging the strengths of deep neural networks, researchers propose the use of a model that combines a type of loss function with a sub-sampling technique. An extensive simulation study has examined the finite sample properties of this model, known as the deep rank-based AFT model, or DeepR-AFT. Results indicate that the model outperforms its counterparts when the predictor is non-linear, while offering improved performance with large sets of factors. Additionally, the model has been tested using two real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness.

Gaia Data Release 3 offers an array of new data products, with a key focus on astrophysical parameters. Produced by the Astrophysical parameters inference system (Apsis) as part of the Gaia Data Processing and Analysis Consortium, this release aims to provide an overview of the included astrophysical parameters and their production methods. By combining BP/RP, RVS, astrometry, and photometry, Apsis derived a range of parameters, including classification, interstellar medium properties, distances, redshifts, and an analysis of outlier sources. Additionally, the astrophysical parameters include a comprehensive set of stellar properties, including temperature, gravity, radius, mass, age, chemical composition, and activity indices, all derived from up to 470 million sources. This catalogue represents the most extensive, uniform collection of astrophysical parameters available, exclusively based on Gaia data.

Our research explores the weak universality of the two-dimensional fractional nonlinear wave equation.  We first establish a criterion that ensures the convergence of invariant measures to the fractional $\Phi_2^4$ model, which holds almost always.  Then, we prove that the associated wave dynamics converge to the renormalized cubic wave equation.  Our result extends the previous work, particularly that of Gubinelli-Koch-Oh, to a case where the nonlinearity exceeds a supercritical threshold.

Building upon Thompson sampling, the Top Two algorithms, initially developed for best arm identification in multi-armed bandit models, have undergone adaptation for parametric arm families. This adaptation involves randomly selecting between two arms, a leader and a challenger, which has yielded positive empirical results. However, theoretical guarantees for best arm identification with fixed confidence levels have only been established in scenarios with Gaussian arms and known variances. This study offers a comprehensive analysis of the Top Two methods, uncovering key properties that define the leader, challenger, and arm distributions. Consequently, it presents theoretically supported Top Two algorithms that can be applied to best arm identification with bounded arm distributions. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the sampling mechanism, which originated from Thompson sampling, can be replaced with alternative methods, including the selection of the empirical best arm.

A novel relativistic theory has been developed for describing the spin properties of vector mesons, specifically utilizing the Kadanoff-Baym equations within the closed-time-path framework. This framework provides a firm foundation for calculating key spin observables, such as the spin density matrix element $\rho_{00}$, which has been formulated into a factorizable form separating momentum and spatial components. Our theory posits that at lower energy levels, the primary contributors to $\rho_{00}$ will be $\phi$-meson fields capable of polarizing quarks and antiquarks in a manner analogous to electromagnetic fields. Crucially, this polarization effect within the $\phi$-meson wave function leads to correlations between the $\phi$-fields that polarize quarks and antiquarks, as reflected in the squared field contributions to $\rho_{00}$. This phenomenon, despite the fluctuating nature of the strong force, can be leveraged to extract fundamental properties of quantum chromodynamics.

In order to develop high-performing sequential recommenders, several novel methods have been proposed to model users' historical behavior patterns. Many existing methods, however, face challenges when applied to new recommendation contexts, as they are based on explicit item identifiers. To overcome this limitation, a new, transferable sequence representation learning approach has been developed, dubbed UniSRec. This innovative method leverages the associated description texts of items to derive adaptable representations that can be applied across diverse recommendation settings. To achieve this, a compact item encoding framework has been designed, incorporating parametric whitening and mixture-of-experts enhanced adaptor. Additionally, two contrastive pre-training tasks have been introduced, which sample multi-domain negatives to learn universal sequence representations. As a result, UniSRec can be seamlessly transferred to new recommendation domains or platforms with minimal parameter adjustments, under either inductive or transductive settings. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets confirm the effectiveness of UniSRec, showcasing its superior transferability, particularly in cross-platform settings. The code and pre-trained model are available at: https://github.com/RUCAIBox/UniSRec.

Graph Neural Networks, which effectively integrate graph information, have become a popular tool for data analysis. Yet, their expressiveness has primarily been examined in the context of graph-level tasks rather than node-level tasks, such as node classification, where missing labels are inferred from observed ones. This paper investigates the expressiveness of GNNs in node classification, which can be seen as a function interpolation problem. By deriving the number of weights and layers necessary for a GNN to approximate a band-limited function, our findings demonstrate that GNNs require significantly fewer weights than fully connected neural networks to achieve an $\epsilon$-approximation - specifically, GNNs need $O((\log \epsilon^{-1})^{d})$ weights trained with $O((\log \epsilon^{-1})^{d})$ samples to approximate a discretized band-limited signal in $\mathbb{R}^d$. This result, which draws a connection between GNN architecture and classical sampling theorems, marks a pioneering attempt in this area.

In numerous domains, sequential data often varies significantly in length, with many sequences being extremely long. To effectively model long-range relationships within such sequences, a crucial tool, neural attention, needs to be developed. Presently, most attention models can only accommodate short sequences, or require the use of chunking or padding techniques to maintain a consistent input length. To address this limitation, we introduce ChordMixer, a straightforward, modular neural network building block that can effectively model attention for sequences with diverse lengths. ChordMixer comprises a fixed, position-wise rotation layer and an element-wise, learnable multilayer perceptron. By iteratively applying ChordMixer modules, a robust, versatile network architecture can be formed that effectively combines input signals with their corresponding targets. Our proposed method has been evaluated on several datasets, including a synthetic task, a document classification task with lengthy texts, and a classification task based on DNA sequences, with the results consistently showing that ChordMixer outperforms existing attention models.

For effective domain generalization, it is essential to develop feature representations that are not specific to a particular domain and capture the underlying semantic characteristics that define an object category. Research has demonstrated that weakly supervised vision-language models, which can learn from minimal, noisy, and cheap text annotations, possess strong semantic understanding capabilities, including the ability to generalize object characteristics across different domains. Nevertheless, as the number of source domains increases, collecting textual annotations for each image in the dataset becomes impractical, which obstructs the application of supervised vision-language approaches in achieving the best possible generalization on an unseen domain. To overcome this limitation, we investigate a new strategy that utilizes multimodal information from pre-trained multimodal networks in an intrinsic manner to facilitate domain generalization. To this end, we introduce INDIGO, a simple yet effective method that leverages the intrinsic multimodality present in pre-trained multimodal networks, along with visual information, to enhance generalization to unseen domains at test time. Our experiments, which involve several Domain Generalization settings, demonstrate state-of-the-art generalization performance on unseen domains. Furthermore, a thorough analysis is provided to gain a deeper understanding of INDIGO.

Modern navigation relies heavily on the capabilities of standalone inertial sensors, which can degrade over time without external reference points. This degradation, often exacerbated by low-cost, low-quality sensors, necessitates the use of estimation algorithms to minimize noise and maximize useful information. Model-based algorithms, traditionally the primary solution, can be less effective due to sensor variability. To address this, researchers have proposed data-driven approaches, which have focused mainly on denoising gyroscope measurements. Accelerometer denoising has proven more challenging, given the unknown effects of gravity. To fill this gap, several learning-based methods have been developed, tested, and compared with existing algorithms. Our results, based on field experiments, indicate that: (i) data-driven models outperform traditional signal processing techniques; (ii) a non-parametric algorithm outperforms all tested deep learning models; (iii) denoising can not only improve signal reconstruction but also significantly reduce errors in navigation-related tasks.

By studying strong gravitational lensing effects around rotating black holes within various gravity theories, researchers can determine the deflection angle, which subsequently influences observable phenomena such as image positions, separation, magnification, and time delays. It has been observed that rotating black holes within the Modified Gravity theory differ more noticeably from those within the General Relativity framework, particularly in the case of SgrA*. These differences, including time delays, can aid in distinguishing Modified Gravity from General Relativity. Additionally, researchers have examined shadow observables, leveraging EHT observations of supermassive black holes, including M87* and SgrA*. This has led to an estimate of the Modified Gravity parameter, yielding an upper limit constraint, with tighter bounds than those derived from the orbital precession of the S2 star.

This discussion delves into the multinomial coefficient and its recurrence relations within the context of generalized quantum deformed algebras. Additionally, it presents the construction of both the $\mathcal{R}(p,q)$-deformed multinomial probability distribution and its negative counterpart, along with the derivation of their recurrence relations. Specific instances of the results, which pertain to quantum algebras already documented in the literature, are derived from the overall framework.

Following the discovery of superconductive twisted bilayer graphene, which marked the beginning of twistronics, researchers have continued to uncover intriguing properties in moiré systems. This study reveals that boron nitride twisted bilayers, with a given moiré periodicity, can exhibit five distinct stackings that preserve the hexagonal symmetry of individual monolayers, contrary to the commonly discussed two. To facilitate accurate description, this research introduces a classification system that clearly identifies twist angles and stacking sequences within hexagonal bilayers with order-3 rotation symmetry. Additionally, density functional theory is employed to analyze the variation in band structure as a function of twist angle across the five boron nitride bilayer stackings. Findings demonstrate that a gap remains indirect at all angles and within any stacking, while specific features remain consistent within the same stacking sequence, regardless of twist angle.

Most interpretability methods for deep neural networks concentrate on the effect that input modifications have on the predicted outcome, often assessed through actual or adjusted gradients. Furthermore, a few approaches adopt a model-agnostic strategy to understand the reasoning behind each prediction. This paper posits that the local geometry of the model parameter space relative to the input can also contribute to better post-hoc explanations. To achieve this, an interpretability method called "geometrically-guided integrated gradients" is introduced, which leverages the calculation of gradients along a linear path as commonly employed in integrated gradient methods. Yet, unlike standard integrated gradients, this method examines the model's behavior from various scaled inputs, capturing the optimal attribution for each input. Experiment results reveal that this novel approach surpasses vanilla and integrated gradients in both subjective and quantitative assessments. Additionally, a "model perturbation" check is proposed as an alternative to the traditionally utilized "model randomization" test.

A novel artificial intelligence-based approach has demonstrated significant potential in enhancing the effectiveness of fluorescence angiography, which has shown promising results in reducing anastomotic leaks. This AI-powered technique aims to overcome the limitations of human interpretation, which varies among surgeons. To achieve this, a deep learning model with a Resnet architecture was trained on a substantial dataset of intraoperative fluorescence angiography videos from a tertiary medical centre. The model was trained on a wide range of images, including both fluorescent and non-fluorescent segments of colon. Validation of the model's performance involved testing it with images from patients not used in the training set, including both images captured with the same equipment and images captured with a different camera. Performance metrics were calculated, and further analysis was conducted using saliency maps. Based on the results, a clear decision boundary was established. Following successful training on 1790 images from 7 patients, the model achieved an impressive 100% accuracy on the training set. Validation results, based on 24 images from 14 patients, revealed an 80% accuracy, with a high level of recall and precision. This achievement has paved the way for the standardization of fluorescence angiography, with a web-based application now available to deploy the AI-powered algorithm.

Convolutional neural networks excel at food image recognition due to their capacity to learn distinctive visual features. However, CNNs struggle with distorted images, which necessitates a novel approach. To address this, a generalized specialist model was designed, combining an ensemble framework with a deep expertise area. This framework allows the models within the ensemble to retain their ability to recognize clean images while also developing shallow skills in classifying images with specific distortions. To further improve the model, a random quality mixup technique, RQMixup, was integrated with snapshot ensembling. During training, RQMixup generates synthetic images that intermix clean and distorted images with varying levels of distortion. This enables each snapshot in the ensemble to develop expertise across multiple distortion levels, while retaining shallow skills in other quality distortions. The diverse expert outputs are then fused to achieve higher accuracy. Notably, this learning process does not incur additional costs, as it can be integrated into a single training process that is compatible with a wide range of CNNs, making it suitable for transfer learning. Experimental results on three real-world food databases, including a Malaysian food database, demonstrated significant improvement in distorted image recognition with comparable performance on pristine images.

A new computationally efficient approach has been devised for assessing the predictive risks associated with Bayesian methods, applicable across a wide range of loss functions. This proposed method leverages posterior covariance, enabling the development of Gibbs and plugin-based generalization error estimators. Key theoretical justifications for the approach are provided, elucidating links between the information criterion, Bayesian sensitivity analysis, and an approximation of leave-one-out cross-validation. Additionally, the potential application of this method in differentially-private learning is explored.

For differential operators with positive-definite symbols on $\mathbb{R}^d$, we examine the behavior of their associated semigroups as time progresses. These semigroups can be described by convolution kernels, which exhibit complex behavior that cannot be determined through standard scaling arguments. We develop a method to analyze the asymptotics of these kernels, specifically their behavior at the origin, for various classes of differential operators. This approach also allows us to study the preservation of asymptotics under perturbations by higher-order differential operators. For instance, we find that the convolution kernel associated with the symbol $P(\xi) = (\eta + \zeta^2)^2 + \eta^4$ behaves like $c_P t^{-5/8}$ as time tends to infinity. This work has implications for understanding the convolution powers of complex functions on $\mathbb{Z}^d$, representing an initial step toward a comprehensive understanding of the associated semigroups.

Even in integrable models, pure ballistic transport is an uncommon phenomenon.  Through a numerical analysis of the Heisenberg chain with an exchange that follows a power-law, $J \propto 1/r^\alpha$, where $r$ denotes distance, it has been demonstrated that with a small amount of spin anisotropy, approximately $\Delta \simeq \exp(-\alpha+2)$, the system exhibits quasiballistic spin transport alongside fermionic excitations that persist until extremely long times, approximately $10^3/J$. This finding is supported by the examination of spin domain dynamics, dynamical spin conductivity, the matrix elements of the spin-current operator, and an analysis of the most conserved operators. Furthermore, the results establish a continuous link between two models that exhibit fully ballistic transport: free particles with nearest-neighbor hopping and the isotropic Haldane-Shastry model.

This paper constructs a cohomology theory for Lie-Yamaguti algebras with their representations, identifies their linear deformations through the second cohomology group, introduces the concept of Rota-Baxter-Nijenhuis structures on these pairs, and analyzes their properties. It also proves that such a structure can result in a compatible pair of Rota-Baxter operators under a given condition. Furthermore, it establishes an equivalence between r-matrix-Nijenhuis and Rota-Baxter-Nijenhuis structures within Lie-Yamaguti algebras.

Modal logic can convey first-order requirements on Kripke frameworks.  A landmark study by Henrik Sahlqvist found a substantial subset of modal formulas that can be translated into equivalent first-order conditions through an algorithm.  Recent advancements have broadened this initial discovery to more intricate modal languages.  This paper builds upon this concept, developing a theorem that correlates Linear-time Temporal Logic with first-order specifications.  LTL, a widely used temporal specification language, extends basic modal logic with temporal operators.  This expansion increases the complexity of formulas with first-order equivalents.  This study identifies a significant subset of LTL formulas, characterized by the use of F, G, X, and U operators.  The central contribution of this paper is demonstrating that these LTL formulas can be translated into equivalent first-order conditions.

Recovering 3D scene structures and camera positions from multiple images, known as Structure-from-Motion, often results in incorrect outcomes due to visually similar scene elements. Existing solutions typically rely on additional constraints or analysis of image features. This paper proposes a different approach that utilizes contextual information within local areas of a scene to improve 3D structure recovery. It introduces a novel concept called a track-community, which groups related image tracks into distinct segments. By applying community detection, the scene is partitioned into segments, with potentially ambiguous areas identified through track analysis. These ambiguities are resolved through pose consistency checks, followed by partial 3D reconstruction within each segment. This is achieved with a new cost function that considers both 3D correspondences and camera pose relationships. Experimental results show that this approach can overcome visually indistinguishable structure limitations, leading to accurate 3D scene recovery.

A method called attention guidance tackles dataset bias in deep learning models that make decisions based on flawed features. For image classification, an interactive human-in-the-loop approach has been developed, allowing users to steer classifiers towards desired image areas, thereby decreasing the impact of co-occurrence bias and enhancing a DNN's transferability and interpretability. This differs from existing methods that demand intricate pixel-level annotations. Our approach involves an easy annotation method via image clicks, paired with an active learning strategy that minimizes the number of annotations needed. Evaluating the proposed system through both numerical analysis and a user study on various datasets, it has been found that our method outperforms existing, non-active-learning methods, which rely heavily on extensive, complex annotations, saving time, effort, and resources. The results also confirm that the developed system is both efficient and dependable.

Introducing Hyper-pool, an innovative, offline, utility-driven algorithm that groups individual ride requests into high-occupancy shared rides. This approach builds upon our previous ExMAS algorithm, which pooled single rides into attractive door-to-door rides, and introduces two new demand-side algorithms. Firstly, it generates rides with a single pick-up and drop-off point that is optimal for all passengers. Secondly, it bundles these rides again, creating 'hyper-pooled' rides that are as efficient as public transportation. Our framework increases the pooling level from the bottom up, ensuring that rides remain attractive at each level. Hyper-pool produces a set of pooled rides per service type, given a travel demand, and is publicly available, making it suitable for large datasets. This method unlocks the full potential of ride-pooling, as seen in our Amsterdam case study, where over 220 passengers were pooled into 40 rides with an average occupancy of 5.8 passengers per vehicle.

To accelerate the time-consuming process of generating optimal architectures, various performance estimation strategies can be employed. This study presents a novel approach called EmProx Score, which shares similarities with Neural Architecture Optimization. It converts candidate architectures into a continuous representation space through an encoder-decoder framework, allowing performance estimation via weighted k-Nearest Neighbors based on known architectures. This method achieves comparable accuracy to existing predictors, such as the MLP used in NAO, but with significantly reduced training times, nearly nine times faster than NAO. Furthermore, it outperforms or matches existing strategies in terms of accuracy, with training times that are up to 80 times faster.

In recent federated learning studies, utilizing large batches has enhanced convergence rates but introduced increased computational requirements. To address this limitation, a novel framework called FedAMD has been devised, which separates participants into anchor and miner groups according to dynamic probabilities. Participants assigned to the anchor group calculate the gradient with large batches, serving as their target. Conversely, clients within the miner group undergo multiple local updates with consecutive mini-batches, with their local updates regulated by a globally derived target, which is an average of all anchor groups' targets. Consequently, the miner group performs near-optimal updates towards the global minimum, which adapts to the global model. Through theoretical analysis, it has been found that FedAMD achieves a convergence rate of $O(1/\epsilon)$ under non-convex objectives with a constant anchor sampling probability. This significantly surpasses the state-of-the-art BVR-L-SGD algorithm, which has a convergence rate of $O(1/\epsilon^{3/2})$, while also reducing the required communication overhead to $O(1/\epsilon)$. Our framework, FedAMD, has been empirically verified on real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and superiority over existing algorithms.

In order to assess the quality of natural language requirements, factors such as sentence length or the use of passive voice are commonly employed. Despite their usefulness, these indicators do not offer a complete understanding of quality factors, which can lead to a fragmented understanding of existing knowledge. This situation prevents the effective utilization and evolution of these factors. To address this, a comprehensive framework consisting of an ontology is proposed. This framework includes a hierarchical structure that categorizes quality factors and related elements, as well as a centralized repository that can be accessed via a web interface. By applying a systematic methodology, an initial version of this framework, as well as the repository and interface, has been created. This initial offering is intended to serve as a foundation for collaborative efforts, with the ultimate goal of establishing a shared understanding of requirements quality factors. It is anticipated that this framework will promote a harmonized perception of requirements quality factors, guide the identification of new factors, and provide a centralized access point for existing knowledge.

In the cascade decay $H\to Z^\ast(\to\tau^+\tau^-)+Z^\ast(\to\tau^+\tau^-)$, both the mass effects of identical particles and leptons must be considered. Since the relevant scale is determined by the off-shellness $p_a^2$ and $p_b^2$ of the $Z$ bosons, which falls within the range $4m_\tau^2\le p_a^2,p_b^2\le (m_H-2m_\tau)^2$, rather than $m_H^2$, lepton mass effects become substantial, especially close to the threshold of the off-shell decays. This study calculates the rates and single-angle decay distributions, comparing them with analogous results for the negligible lepton mass case, specifically the non-identical particle decays $H\to Z^\ast(\to e^+e^-)+Z^\ast(\to\mu^+\mu^-)$.

This study showcases the value of the vast data products provided in the Gaia Data Release 3, specifically the detailed astrophysical parameters for approximately half a billion stars. By leveraging these resources, we have created six diverse datasets that can be utilized across various astrophysical contexts. Our methods involve querying relevant tables within the Gaia DR3, corroborating our findings with both the Gaia catalogue and external data. This research yields six high-quality datasets that cover a wide range of stars, which can be accessed through the Gaia archive. Focusing on three extensive datasets, we examine young stars, stars with a certain spectral type, and ultra-compact dwarfs. Additionally, we identify 15,740 genuine carbon stars, 5,863 solar-analogues, and provide a unified set of parameters for the Spectro Photometric Standard Stars. Furthermore, we utilize these datasets to analyze the rotation of the Milky Way, examine known exoplanet systems, determine the ages of certain unseen companions, and even predict the colors of the Sun across different wavelengths.

FLASH radiotherapy, which involves ultra-high dose rate electron beams, is gaining significance in preclinical cancer research.  Unfortunately, no real-time dose monitoring device exists due to the high dose rates used.  This study describes the development of a beam current transformer, encompassing component selection, shielding, and a trans-impedance circuit-based front-end electronics.  The BCT prototype can monitor beam currents ranging from 1.2 microamps to 200 milliamperes with improved sensitivity, possessing a rise time constant below 20 nanoseconds and a signal droop rate below 0.05% per microsecond.  Initial in-situ measurements have also been conducted.  Our ultimate goal is to integrate this BCT system with an ionisation chamber, which monitors beam shape and position, to create a reliable real-time dose monitoring system.

A groundbreaking method has been created for analyzing single-channel partial wave reactions that rely on energy, rather than developing complex theoretical models. Traditionally, researchers constructed models, solved them, adjusted parameters, and reconstructed partial waves. This new method involves expressing partial waves as a Laurent series with a fast-converging expansion, known as a Pietarinen expansion, which can be applied to any reaction. By determining singularities, such as poles and branch-points, this method avoids the complexity of constructing a theoretical model. It has been successfully applied to $K \Lambda$ photoproduction, which has an extensive dataset. However, this method also involves a complicated formalism with numerous parameters, requiring simplifications, such as amplitude+partial wave analysis, to be handled with current computer capabilities.

Fermi J1544-0649, a previously unseen high-energy source, caught scientists' attention with a flare detected in 2017.  It exhibited blazar-like behavior during this time, characterized by variability and a distinct energy distribution.  Outside of this flare, Fermi J1544-0649 appeared relatively quiet, resembling a regular galaxy, with minimal high-energy activity over a decade.  This pattern, coupled with the detection of absorption lines, led researchers to investigate the'misaligned blazar' theory.  By analyzing data from 2018-2020, scientists identified four distinct jet components associated with Fermi J1544-0649, yielding an estimated viewing angle between 3.7-7.4 degrees.  This finding suggested that Fermi J1544-0649 might have an unusually low duty cycle for gamma-ray emission, with the upper viewing angle limit supporting the'misaligned blazar' hypothesis.  Continued multi-wavelength observations after 2018 confirmed that Fermi J1544-0649 remained relatively quiet, with no high-energy activity detected.  Notably, a neutrino search yielded an intriguing 3.1 sigma significance.

Semi-supervised learning can alleviate the reliance on labeled data through strategic approaches. It has been successfully applied to structured data like images and text, utilizing pre-trained models or data enhancement. However, these methods become ineffective when domain structures are absent. Pseudo-labeling methods, despite their simplicity, can be applied universally without domain assumptions, yet they remain susceptible to noise and inaccurate assignments. This paper presents a solution, Confident Sinkhorn Allocation, which selectively assigns confident labels and optimizes label distribution through transport theory, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods in this critical area. Our implementation is available on GitHub.

Given the equation $\zeta^k(s) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \tau_k(n) n^{-s}, \Re s > 1$, three conditional results are provided regarding the sum $$\sum_{n\le X} \tau_3(n) \tau_3(n+h)$$, with numerical verifications supporting the method. Firstly, a conditional proof is given for the main term of this sum for $h=1$ under an averaged distribution assumption for the three-fold divisor function. Secondly, a derivation is provided for the leading asymptotics of this sum, applicable for any composite shift $h$. Thirdly, a complete expansion is obtained for the polynomial main term, also for $h=1$, through the delta-method, showing that the results match. Furthermore, an unconditional result of Heath-Brown is refined, with a numerical study of the error terms showing square-root cancellation. This method, which relies on congruences, is elementary, particularly for $h=1$, and agrees with prior predictions, heuristic arguments, and computations. This procedure can be applied generally to yield the main term with a power-saving error term for correlations of the form $\sum_{n\le X} \tau_k(n) f(n+h)$, with any composite shift $h$ and any arithmetic function $f(n)$.

A method for generating photons from vacuum through time-modulated coupling between a quantum system, an ancilla, and a cavity is proposed. This method involves modulating an artificial 2-level atom, referred to as a t-qubit, with the ancilla serving as a mediator between the cavity and t-qubit. It is found that even with significant detuning, tripartite entangled states with a small number of photons can be generated from the ground state through resonant modulation, provided certain conditions regarding the t-qubit's frequencies are met. This method's effectiveness is validated through numerical simulations, demonstrating that it can withstand common sources of dissipation.

Recent interest in quantized neural networks stems from their ability to significantly reduce memory and computational requirements during inference.  While it has long been believed that quantization serves as an implicit regularizer, enhancing neural network generalizability, this concept has yet to be formally proven.  This paper examines binary weight neural networks through stochastic rounding, analyzing how probability distributions propagate through different layers.  A novel, continuous neural network, dubbed a quasi neural network, is introduced to approximate this behavior.  By deriving the neural tangent kernel for this quasi neural network, it is shown that the NTK's eigenvalues decrease at an exponential rate, comparable to that of a Gaussian kernel with a randomized scale.  This suggests that the function space spanned by binary weight neural networks is a subset of that spanned by real-valued weight neural networks.  Experimental validation confirms the efficacy of the proposed quasi neural network, with binary weight neural networks also exhibiting lower generalization errors compared to their real-valued counterparts.  This finding parallels the difference between Gaussian and Laplace kernels.

In this paper, a thorough investigation into the production of doubly-charmed baryons through $Z$ boson decay is conducted, utilizing the principles of nonrelativistic QCD factorization. By incorporating the di-quark states $(cc)[^3S_1]_{\bar{\textbf{3}}}$ and $(cc)[^1S_0]_{{\textbf{6}}}$, predictions indicate that the branching ratio for $\mathcal{B}_{Z \to \Xi_{cc}+X}$ falls within the $10^{-5}$ order, rendering it experimentally measurable. By comparing this with the $\Lambda^{+}_{c}$ yield in $Z$ decay, it is forecast that $\mathcal{R}_{\Xi_{cc}^{+}}$ equals $(0.85^{+0.10}_{-0.07}) \times 10^{-4}$, and $\mathcal{R}_{\Xi_{cc}^{++}}$ equals $(1.70^{+0.20}_{-0.14}) \times 10^{-4}$, values that significantly differ from SELEX measurements yet align with LHCb and Belle collaborations' data.

A bipartite quantum state that can retain all the information about an unknown action on it, referred to as a system, is called faithful.  Research has shown that there is an important connection between the faithfulness of a quantum state and the invertibility of a corresponding transformation, known as the Jamiolkowski map.  This connection, initially demonstrated by D'Ariano and Presti, has been beneficial for a method called ancilla-assisted process tomography, although their proof contained an error as it assumed that certain types of operations do not increase the overall trace.  We provide a complete proof of this connection and also explore a more general concept, referred to as sensitivity, which describes how a quantum state can be altered by different actions.  By examining the relationships between these properties, we have found that there are specific classes of quantum channels that can be used to characterize whether a quantum state is faithful or sensitive.  This research has shown that there are only two types of quantum states required for this characterization, which can provide insights into the structure of different types of channels.  For example, it has been discovered that unital channels can only be detected using bipartite states that do not have any local classical observable.

As technology advances, credit card fraud has become a significant issue that can be exploited, making it crucial to establish a reliable method for identifying such scams. Machine learning algorithms, which prioritize prediction accuracy, can be an effective tool in this pursuit. Nonetheless, there's a potential pitfall: if a dataset has an uneven distribution of classes, with one class significantly outnumbering the others, this can lead to poor performance from learning models that predict all labels as the majority class. This can hinder their ability to make accurate, generalized predictions. To mitigate this issue, we employed a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to create a substantial number of authentic, synthetic instances of the minority class, which can help counterbalance the class imbalance and enhance the learning process.

Given two Hecke eigenforms $h_1$ and $h_2$ in the Kohnen plus space of half-integral weight, let $I_n(h_1)$ and $I_n(h_2)$ denote their respective Duke-Imamoglu-Ikeda lifts, which are Siegel cusp forms with respect to $Sp_n(\ZZ)$. Additionally, let $E_{n/2+1/2}$ represent the Cohen Eisenstein series of weight $n/2+1/2$. Using this, we express the Rankin-Selberg convolution $R(s,I_n(h_1),I_n(h_2))$ as a Dirichlet series $D(s,h_1,h_2,E_{n/2+1/2})$, similar to a triple convolution product. This formula can be used to prove mass equidistribution for the Duke-Imamoglu-Ikeda lift, under the assumption that $D(s,h_1,h_1,E_{n/2+1/2})$ is holomorphic.

A cutting-edge method for automatically calibrating ultrasound probes during tracking has been developed.  A custom phantom with nine cone structures of varying heights has been designed, utilizing their tips as reference points for cross-sweep matching.  These tips are identified using a deep learning-based segmentation approach, followed by tracking across successive ultrasound frames.  Robust calibration estimates are produced through RANSAC, with further refinement achieved through image-based techniques.  This phantom, capable of being 3D printed, boasts several advantages over existing methods, with the phantom's design and accompanying algorithm freely available online.  Its ease of use is enhanced, as it doesn't necessitate a tracking target, and it can be used with various probes from different vendors, as demonstrated through our experiments.  Our approach yields calibration results comparable to those obtained by an expert in the field.

In this research, we examine how cosmic microwave background polarization data can verify potential irregularities in temperature data, specifically concerning large-scale correlations, quadrupole-octupole alignment, point-parity imbalance, and hemispherical power imbalance. Utilizing simulations that mimic data from three major experiments, we investigate how current and future data can influence these anomalies. Our analysis reveals that polarization data can independently verify these irregularities with a low correlation coefficient, especially concerning point-parity imbalance. Future data, such as that from LiteBIRD, will significantly reduce errors on these irregularities, with LiteBIRD offering a threefold reduction for hemispherical power imbalance and point-parity imbalance, as well as a 26-fold reduction for large-scale correlation irregularities. Although LiteBIRD's influence on quadrupole-octupole alignment is less apparent, it will allow for a more precise estimate with an improvement factor of over 100. Meanwhile, data from the Cosmology Large Angular Scale Surveyor will have an intermediate effect.

In cases where the slow-roll parameter $\epsilon_H$ is less than $H^2/M_{\rm Pl}^2$, significant inflaton fluctuations after horizon crossing can lead to eternal inflation, even if these fluctuations aren't enough to create a black hole through density fluctuations. These fluctuations can, however, produce notable density fluctuations in radiation as the number of degrees of freedom increases rapidly, as predicted by the distance conjecture. We propose that the condition requiring that radiation density fluctuations don't produce a black hole until the end of inflation is equivalent to the condition that eternal inflation won't occur. When radiation doesn't produce a black hole, even if the number of degrees of freedom increases, the information paradox doesn't arise if $\epsilon_H$ is greater than $10^{-7} (H^2/ M_{\rm Pl}^2)$ and the time scale is shorter than $10^4 (M_{\rm Pl}/H^2)$. Regardless of the presence of the information paradox, an observer won't be able to gather enough information, which aligns with the principle of complementarity.

Given any non-erasing monoid morphism $\sigma$ that maps strings from one alphabet to strings from another, it generates a specific transformation, denoted as $\sigma_X^{\cal M}$, which transfers measures between the spaces of measures on a particular symbolic sequence $X$ and its transformed version $\sigma(X)$. This transformation is further studied, with $\sigma_X^{\cal M}$ being proven continuous, linear, functorial, and surjective. Moreover, an efficient method is proposed to compute the transferred measures. Additionally, it is demonstrated that if a non-erasing morphism $\sigma$ can be recognized within a specific symbolic sequence $X$, then $\sigma_X^{\cal M}$ will be a one-to-one correspondence. The term "recognizable" refers to a fundamental concept in symbolic dynamics, which has undergone various transformations and refinements over time. To establish this result, it is proven that a non-erasing morphism $\sigma$ can be recognized within some symbolic sequence $X$ if and only if it satisfies two specific conditions: it induces an injective mapping between the orbits of $X$ and $\sigma(X)$, and it preserves the periodicity of any periodic words within $X$.

We extend the perturbative quantum field theory framework, as initially proposed for the pure Yang-Mills model, to show that tree-level contributions indeed do not yield anomalies. Furthermore, we will establish a more comprehensive version of this gauge invariance property.

In various technology stacks, package managers play a vital role as mediators that verify, install, configure, or uninstall application dependencies. Diverse technology stacks have led to multiple package managers with varying functionalities. Our investigation, based on a study of Stack Overflow content, reveals that package management features significantly impact end-user experiences. However, it remains unclear what specific challenges end-users face and what information is necessary to resolve these issues. This study analyzed 1,131 Stack Overflow questions related to three prominent package managers, Maven, npm, and NuGet, to identify issue patterns, underlying causes, and resolutions. Our findings indicate that end-users experience difficulties with package manager tool usage, with approximately 64-72% struggling. The main causes of these issues include inadequate instructions and error messages. External link sharing emerged as a common method for resolving package manager problems, with links pointing to official documentation, tutorials, and other resources being frequently shared.

A torus associated with a commutative \'etale algebra $L$ over a global field $k$ is considered of Kummer type if every factor of $L$ corresponds to a cyclic Kummer extension. This paper computes the Tate-Shafarevich group for tori based on previously established research, primarily that of Bayer-Fluckiger, T.-Y. Lee, and Parimala, along with further contributions from T.-Y. Lee. Additionally, an effective algorithm using SAGE is introduced, which can compute the Tate-Shafarevich group when each factor of $L$ is contained within a specific bicyclic extension of $k$.

New biological techniques, like multi-way chromosome conformation capture, necessitate the creation of methods for studying multiple interactions simultaneously. Hypergraphs, being mathematically manageable, can accurately represent and analyze these complex interactions. This paper introduces the Hypergraph Analysis Toolbox, a software application that facilitates visualization and analysis of multiple interactions within intricate systems.

We prove that for any pair of minimal models associated with a generalized log canonical pair, there exist birational models with low discrepancy that can be related via a chain of flop operations with a specific property.

To reduce the impact of anomalies, kNN ensembles create a group of closest data points to a new sample point, using a voting system based on the labels of surrounding data points, to estimate its unknown category. Traditional kNN methods find the k closest data points within a specific range using a distance metric. However, these methods may fail when test data follows a pattern that lies outside the sphere of nearest neighbors. Moreover, these methods can produce poor ensembles if many base kNN learners have high error rates. To overcome these challenges, an improved ensemble method based on an optimal neighborhood rule is introduced, which identifies neighbors in stages. Starting with the closest point, it selects subsequent data points that are closest to previously chosen points, until k points are identified. Each ensemble model is built using a bootstrapped sample combined with a random subset of features. After building a sufficient number of base models, the top-performing models are chosen based on their performance on unseen data.

In modern applications like social networks, healthcare, and finance, point process data have become increasingly common. However, traditional recurrent neural networks may fail to capture complex, non-stationary relationships within this data due to their inherent structures. Instead, we utilize a different approach based on neural networks that represent the influence kernel, a fundamental concept in point process modeling. Our method introduces a novel low-rank decomposition technique that enables efficient point process modeling using deep neural networks, offering improved computational efficiency and better performance. Additionally, we incorporate a log-barrier penalty to maintain the non-negativity constraint of conditional intensity, resulting in a more effective point process model. Our proposed method achieves superior results compared to current state-of-the-art models, as demonstrated on simulated and real-world data.

This study presents an end-to-end neural mapping technique for camera localization that transforms an entire scene into a grid of compact latent codes. Using these codes, a Transformer-based decoder can accurately predict 3D coordinates for specific pixels. Traditional camera localization methods, however, rely on storing 3D point clouds with associated per-point features, which can occupy an excessive amount of storage space, often multiple gigabytes per scene. While compression can be employed, it inevitably results in a notable decrease in performance, particularly at high compression ratios. NeuMap circumvents this limitation by leveraging 1) learnable latent codes to store scene data and 2) a scene-independent Transformer-based decoder that infers coordinates for a given pixel. The design also enables robust matching priors through extensive training with large-scale data, as well as efficient optimization of codes for new scenes with fixed network weights. Thorough evaluations across five benchmarks reveal that NeuMap surpasses other coordinate regression methods substantially, achieving comparable performance to feature matching methods, albeit with a significantly smaller scene representation. For instance, NeuMap achieved 39.1% accuracy on the Aachen night benchmark using merely 6MB of data, whereas competing methods often require 100MB or multiple gigabytes, failing under high compression settings. The NeuMap codes can be accessed on GitHub.

We examine the primary challenge of online control for linear systems from two distinct perspectives: minimizing regret and competitive analysis. Our findings show that the best competitive strategy can be closely approximated using a specific, adaptable control framework, known as disturbance-action control policies. Utilizing this insight, we demonstrate that multiple proposed online control methods can simultaneously achieve superior outcomes: they can obtain near-optimal results compared to the best DAC policy, determined after the fact, while also offering an optimal competitive ratio, with an error that grows at a slower rate as time progresses. We also conclude that it's feasible to attain near-optimal results compared to the best competitive strategy, even when the system's dynamics are unknown, or if a pre-existing controller that maintains stability is unavailable.

Discovering optimal update rules for black-box optimization methods like evolution strategies, which lack gradient access, is a goal that can be achieved using meta-learning.  Since black-box methods often rely on general, yet inflexible learning dynamics, our proposed approach aims to overcome these limitations.  We propose using a self-attention-based search strategy, which inherently ensures that the derived update rules are unaffected by the candidate solution ordering.  Our method demonstrates that learning this system on a small set of low-dimensional optimization problems can result in generalizable evolution strategies that can solve unseen optimization tasks.  Furthermore, our proposed method can even outperform established neuroevolution baselines on a range of tasks.  As additional contributions, we also analyze the impact of our method's components, reverse-engineer our learned strategy, and show that it's feasible to train an evolution strategy using the learned update rule as a self-driving mechanism.

Current text-to-SQL studies have a limitation as they typically involve a single task with a pre-defined dataset. However, real-world applications often present a sequence of tasks, leading to issues with insufficient supervised data and the associated costs of frequent model updates. Insufficient data tends to result in overfitting on unfamiliar tasks, while the costs make it impractical to incorporate past tasks, leading to a loss of learned SQL patterns and database schema. To overcome these issues, this study suggests integrating semi-supervised learning and continual learning within a sequence of text-to-SQL tasks. It introduces two solutions: Vanilla, which incorporates self-training with predicted pseudo-labeled data, and episodic memory replay to balance model efficiency with past performance. The second, more refined solution, SFNet, leverages the relationship between CL and SSL, utilizing past data to enhance current learning, while also incorporating high-quality, stored pseudo instances to improve future replay. Experimental results on two datasets indicate that SFNet surpasses SSL-only and CL-only baselines across multiple metrics.

Examination of the Ground Wide Angle Camera's archive uncovered 43 white light flares originating from 43 stars, with three being homologous events, one featuring a 13 minute quasi-periodic pulsation, and 19 newly discovered active stars. Analysis of available light curves from 41 stars yielded 931 stellar flares, 34 stars' rotational or orbital periods were measured, revealing 33 less than 5.4 days, while ephemerides were obtained for three eclipsing binaries. Combining these findings with low resolution spectra, it was discovered that 43 stars' $L_{\rm H\alpha}/L_{\rm bol}$ were within the saturation region on the rotation-activity diagram. Medium-resolution LAMOST spectrum analysis confirmed Star #3 as a binary system with active components, and 13 stars' flare frequency distributions showed that detected flares can occur 0.5-9.5 times per year. Furthermore, study of these distributions indicated that some stars' flares could potentially damage ozone layers on habitable planets, though none would be sufficient to initiate prebiotic chemistry.

In multi-domain recommendation systems, users interact with various marketing strategies across different scenarios, leading to diverse demands that need to be addressed simultaneously. However, conventional graph neural network-based methods have limitations, as they typically handle each domain separately, failing to utilize cross-domain user behaviors, or they learn a shared model that neglects users' unique preferences within each domain. To address these issues, learning separate user representations that reflect their domain-specific preferences can be beneficial. We introduce $\mathsf{H^3Trans}$, a novel framework that employs a hierarchical hypergraph network for correlative preference transfer across multiple domains. $\mathsf{H^3Trans}$ consolidates multi-domain user feedback into a unified graph, enabling full exploitation of users' cross-domain behaviors. It incorporates two hyperedge-based modules: the dynamic item transfer module, which eliminates item representation discrepancies across domains, and the adaptive user aggregation module, which aggregates users' preferences across domains, leveraging high-order connections among them. Our experimental results demonstrate that $\mathsf{H^3Trans}$ significantly outperforms existing methods on both public datasets and large-scale production datasets.

The incorporation of Yukawa interactions within Grand Unified Theories, specifically those based on $SO(10)$, can predict novel scalar particles that may have observable effects.  We investigated this possibility within a realistic, renormalizable model, focusing on color sextet diquark scalars.  The model's particle spectrum consists of five sextets, each with unique characteristics, including their couplings with quarks.  We evaluated their contributions to neutral meson-antimeson mixing and processes that violate baryon number, such as neutron-antineutron oscillation, which arises due to a $B-L$ violating trilinear coupling.  However, this process is limited by perturbativity, leading to stringent constraints on the sextet masses.  Using realistic model parameters, we derived mass limits, finding that certain sextets cannot be simultaneously light.  As a result, observable $n$-$\bar{n}$ oscillations may not occur in near-future experiments.  We also propose an alternative scenario, where a sub-GUT scale scalar can potentially explain the observed baryon asymmetry of the universe.

To achieve cost-effectiveness, mobile network operators are pushing 5G and beyond networks towards more flexible, adaptable, and resource-efficient deployments that can handle diverse user needs. We propose that cloud-native, zero-touch orchestration systems, equipped with end-to-end monitoring, can meet these demands. This live demonstration, built on a cloud-native 5G test platform with wireless transmissions, showcases how intent-based requirements can be fulfilled by dynamically relocating container-based user applications. As a result, we conduct an experimental validation to prove how our platform supports flexible, agile, and efficient 5G network deployments.

Researchers have been studying how laser-generated bubbles within a confined microfluidic device can be used as a driving force for micro-jets, specifically for needle-free jet injectors. We have investigated bubble formation using a continuous-wave laser and a pulsed laser within an open-ended microfluidic capillary, allowing us to compare bubble generation under different time scales. The bubble's growth rate plays a crucial role, as it determines the available energy for subsequent liquid jet formation. We observed that bubble growth increases proportionally with the delivered energy for both types of lasers, with equal absorption coefficient resulting in similar bubble growth. However, CW lasers require more optical energy due to heat dissipation, while also exhibiting slightly more size variability under identical initial conditions, likely due to the stochastic nature of thermocavitation.

Stable subordinators with an index $\alpha$ within the interval $(0,1)$
generate remarkable Gibbs partitions that have well understood properties.
These partitions can be used to derive complex asymptotic results with
considerable ease, making them applicable to a broad range of stochastic
processes, tree/graph growth models, and Bayesian statistics. Specifically,
this work extends the well-known models based on the two-parameter
Poisson-Dirichlet distribution, focusing on embedding essential operations
within this framework. We address the challenge of applying the dual, infinite
block, coagulation/fragmentation results of Jim Pitman's 1999 study, which
explores coagulation using independent two-parameter Poisson-Dirichlet
distributions, to all Gibbs models. By doing so, we create nested families of
Gibbs partitions, including mass partitions, that can be applied across any
$0<\beta<\alpha<1$ interval. We primarily investigate the fragmentation
operations, which remain independent, and their resulting Gibbs partitions.
