involves transforming the SDE into a discrete-time model, designing efficient 
particle filters for the new model, and developing a scheme that converges 
weakly at order 1. A class of space-sequential particle filters is also 
introduced, which leverages the model's structure to improve performance for 
high-dimensional systems. The effectiveness of this new approach is 
demonstrated through simulations of a stochastic Lorenz 96 system, which show 
that estimation errors remain approximately constant while computational cost 
increases polynomially with system dimension. This paper provides a comprehensive 
framework for discrete-time filtering in continuous-time systems described by 
SDEs, and proves that, under certain conditions, the discrete-time model's 
posterior distributions converge to the continuous-time model's posterior 
distributions. This result is applicable to any weakly-convergent discretisation 
scheme, not just the specific scheme and particle filters discussed here.

It is thought that supernovae and star outflows are responsible for producing interstellar dust particles of considerable size. The fragmentation of these larger particles, which have undergone stochastic acceleration, is believed to produce smaller dust grains. To study stochastic acceleration, researchers developed new numerical methods by integrating magnetohydrodynamic and particle-in-cell models into the astrophysical fluid code RAMSES. This model represents dust particles as large,'super' particles, which are influenced by aerodynamic drag and the Lorentz force. The numerical model was tested under different physical conditions, allowing for the validation of the technique and exploration of possible acceleration mechanisms. A final test, which also serves as a basis for further research, involved simulating decaying MHD turbulence in conditions similar to those found in cold, neutral interstellar medium. The results show that, under such conditions, grains measuring 1-2 micrometers in size can be accelerated to velocities significantly exceeding their shattering limits. This is observed for both charged and neutral grains, albeit with distinct differences. Although neutral grains exhibit higher peak velocities, charged grains display a longer, exponential tail, which indicates increased gas-grain interaction. This, however, provides charged grains with protection from shattering. The study also highlights the link between the simulated results and pristine, pre-solar dust grains, which appear to have remained intact over their lifetimes.
This document outlines technical specifics for the Hybrid-AIM simulator, which was employed in Sharon and Stone (2017) and Parks-Young and Sharon (2022).

It has been demonstrated that there are no odd-dimensional, compact, and stable minimal immersions present within the product of two complex projective spaces. Furthermore, we establish that the sole compact, stable, and minimal immersions found within the product of a quaternionic projective space and any other Riemannian manifold are direct products of quaternionic projective subspaces combined with compact, stable, and minimal immersions of the second manifold within the given product. These results serve to generalize previous findings by the second-named author, which pertained to low-dimensional or low-codimensional immersions, to now encompass immersions of arbitrary dimensions. Additionally, we also prove that within the product of an octonionic projective plane and any other Riemannian manifold, the sole compact, stable, and minimal immersions are direct products of octonionic projective subspaces combined with compact, stable, and minimal immersions of the second manifold within the given product.

This paper constructs an anticyclotomic Euler system for the adjoint representation of elliptic modular forms transferred to an imaginary quadratic field, and also connects it to a $p$-adic $L$-function resulting from unitary groups' $p$-adic $L$-functions. Consequently, we establish new instances of the Bloch-Kato conjecture in rank zero, along with divisibility towards the Iwasawa main conjecture.

This study focuses on resolving the issue of mapping areas actively, which involves planning a sequence of observations given a set constraint like travel distance. It specifically examines active occupancy grid mapping using range sensors like LiDAR or depth cameras. Current leading approaches optimize measures of information, relating occupancy grid probabilities to sensor readings. However, the non-smooth aspect of ray tracing within grid representations leads to non-differentiable objectives, requiring existing methods to search for optimal paths among possible trajectories. A novel, differentiable approximation of mutual information between grid maps and ray-based observations is proposed, enabling gradient-based optimization over the continuous space of sensor positions. The resulting approach leads to more informative observations, while avoiding obstacles and collisions. The proposed method is illustrated through experiments in simulated and real-world environments, including 2-D and 3-D settings.

To reveal minute movements in videos, researchers employ motion magnification techniques, which typically fall under two primary approaches: Eulerian and Lagrangian. The former involves processing image pixels directly, whereas the latter utilizes optical flow techniques to trace and amplify pixel paths. This study focuses on facial microexpressions, which are short-lived and spatially confined facial movements difficult to detect. A novel approach for enhancing facial micromovements is presented, which involves fine-tuning a deep learning model for facial optical flows by integrating ground truth obtained from a variationally dense inverse search algorithm. This approach yields accurate and efficient optical flows for facial videos. Moreover, since facial micromovements are spatially and temporally localized, the proposed method involves decomposing the optical flow field into sparse components in both space and time, leading to a double sparse decomposition. The resulting decomposition is then utilized to magnify micro-motions in specific facial areas, utilizing a novel forward warping strategy involving triangular image grid splitting and barycentric interpolation. The approach is demonstrated to be highly effective through various examples.

Recent advancements in high-pressure synthesis techniques have enabled researchers to produce samples on the indium-rich side of (Pb,In)Te, which exhibit higher superconducting transition temperatures than their lead-rich counterparts. This study examines the temperature dependence of the London penetration depth in In$_{0.8}$Pb$_{0.2}$Te, which features a bulk onset superconducting transition at approximately 4.75 K. The obtained results suggest a fully gapped BCS-like superconducting state, which contradicts the possibility of odd-parity, nontrivial $A_{2u}$ pairing but does not exclude odd-parity $A_{1u}$ pairing. Moreover, critical magnetic field values and other relevant superconducting parameters are reported at temperatures below 1 K.

Collaborative human-AI creativity requires humans and AI to co-create products
together, necessitating interaction dynamics such as turn-taking, contribution
types, and communication. These dynamics are crucial for co-creative systems,
yet there is limited research on interaction design, which is often overlooked
in existing co-creative systems. Co-creativity research has primarily focused on
AI capabilities, but this paper emphasizes the importance of interaction design
by introducing the Co-Creative Framework for Interaction (COFI). COFI serves as
a model for researchers to explore interaction possibilities, analyze existing
systems, and identify areas for improvement. We employed COFI to analyze 92
co-creative systems, demonstrating its effectiveness in categorizing interaction
models. Our findings highlight opportunities to redefine interaction models,
ultimately enhancing human-AI partnerships by facilitating better user-AI
communication.

A unified approach is presented for combining mixed-space quantum representations in Condensed Matter Physics and Quantum Field Theory. This unified framework is built on the ability to express any quantum operator, for bosons, fermions, and spin systems, in terms of a universal basis operator involving mixed Hilbert spaces. This operator is derived from momentum and position operators, which are fundamental to Condensed Matter Physics, and are related to creation and annihilation operators in Quantum Field Theory. The expansion coefficients are obtained from the Fourier transform of the Wigner quantum distribution function. This approach enables various transformations, including fermionization and bosonization, to be performed. Additionally, unitary transformations, such as the Bogoliubov transformation, and matrix-based transformations, like the Jordan-Schwinger transformation, are employed to simplify calculations. It is demonstrated that the coherent states formulation is a special case of this unified approach, and a new formulation of Quantum Field Theory is suggested. Furthermore, the approach is extended to nonequilibrium quantum transport physics, which involves non-Hermitian operators and time-reversal symmetry breaking.

This investigation focuses on weighted $L_p$ affine surface areas, which are significant components of the $L_p$ Steiner formula derived from $L_p$ Brunn-Minkowski theory. We demonstrate that these areas are valuations for convex bodies and derive isoperimetric inequalities. Furthermore, we establish connections between these areas and $f$-divergences, including Kullback-Leibler and R\'enyi divergences, which are related to cone measures of convex bodies and their polar counterparts.

Research has focused on manganese-based nitride antiperovskites, such as Mn$_3$NiN, which feature a triangular magnetic ordering over their kagome lattice. Due to frustration, these materials adopt non-trivial magnetic interactions, requiring noncollinear magnetic configurations. The associated electronic interactions, influenced by factors like epitaxial strain, significantly impact their microscopic and macroscopic properties. In our investigation, we examined how epitaxial strain, confined to the (111) plane, affects magnetic and crystallographic symmetries, while adjusting ionic and electronic interactions. Our findings indicate a linear band structure energy shift and proportional changes in states near the Fermi level under applied strain. Notably, compressive strain shortens Mn-Mn distances but expands stacked kagome lattices, increasing states near the Fermi level. However, the anomalous Hall conductivity exhibits non-linear behavior, nearly vanishing under tensile strain, but increasing by up to 26% for compressive strain near $-$1.5%. This phenomenon is attributed to non-divergent Berry curvature within the kagome plane, which is heightened under compressive but reduced under tensile strain.

Determining non-Gaussian patterns from complex structure formation is essential for fully exploiting future large-scale surveys. However, analyzing observational data remains a significant challenge due to theoretical and computational obstacles. A new approach has been developed to address this challenge, utilizing 3D wavelets to extract key statistics from matter fields. These statistics are calculated by averaging the complex modulus of wavelet transforms, which are constructed on a spherical grid. In tests, these statistics outperformed existing methods, providing state-of-the-art constraints on key cosmological parameters, such as neutrino masses. Moreover, they improved constraints by 5-10 times compared to traditional methods.

For ranked tree-child networks chosen at random, we derive probability laws governing how frequently certain patterns on their fringes appear. Our findings generalize previous work by Bienvenu et al. (2022) on 'cherry' patterns. We found that for patterns of height $1$ and $2$, there are distinct possibilities: either such patterns are common, resulting in linear averages and normal probability laws, or they are relatively rare, resulting in constant averages and Poisson laws, or nearly non-existent, resulting in averages converging to $0$ and degenerate laws. We speculate that our observed possibilities are exhaustive for any fringe pattern.

Following new laws, there is growing interest in machine unlearning, which involves
removing specific training samples from predictive models, treating them as if they
never existed. Unlearning may be needed due to corrupted data, adversarial attacks,
or users' changing privacy needs. For some models, such as k-NN, removing the closest
sample is sufficient. However, this is not applicable to more complex models. Recent
approaches leveraging optimization-based updates are limited by their poor performance
with high-dimensional models. We developed a new method, based on a conditional
independence coefficient, called L-CODEC, which identifies key model parameters for
individual samples, eliminating the need for matrix inversion. This makes our method
suitable for deep learning, and other applications like computer vision, which would
otherwise be impractical. Our approach outperforms alternatives, enabling approximate
unlearning in previously infeasible scenarios, such as face recognition, person
re-identification, and certain natural language processing models. The code is publicly
available at https://github.com/vsingh-group/LCODEC-deep-unlearning/.

Research has not thoroughly addressed machine learning (ML) in requirements engineering. Developing ML systems poses various challenges, but focusing on ML in RE could lead to more dependable systems. A catalogue of 45 concerns, developed from past studies and real-world experience, has been proposed for ML systems. These concerns are categorized under five key aspects: objectives, user experience, infrastructure, model, and data. For example, concerns such as execution engine and telemetry relate to infrastructure, while explainability and reproducibility are crucial for model development. A focus group involving eight professionals validated the significance, usefulness, and practicality of our catalogue. Their input allowed for catalogue improvement and verification of its relevance. This research contributes by providing a set of validated concerns, categorized by perspective, which can aid requirements engineers in specifying ML systems.

An in-depth examination is conducted on the role of Renyi relative entropy situated between two elements in AdS/CFT and finite-dimensional holographic quantum error correction models. A suitable modification of Renyi relative entropy is proposed for finite-dimensional von Neumann algebras, specifically in the context of operator algebra quantum error correction. It is then demonstrated that bulk and boundary Renyi relative entropies are equivalent to specific conditions, including state encoding, Ryu-Takayanagi formula, and subregion duality. These findings expand on previous equivalency theorems, and Renyi relative entropy is also defined in terms of modular operators, which is naturally suited for finite-dimensional holographic quantum error correction. Additionally, numerical calculations are performed on a holographic random tensor network to gain insight into corrections to bulk and boundary Renyi relative entropy.

Massive galaxies' life cycles are influenced by low-excitation radio galaxies, but their origins and impact on early galaxies are not well understood. We analyzed 10,481 low-excitation radio galaxies from the LOFAR Two-meter Sky Survey, covering 25 square degrees, to measure their radio luminosity function out to a redshift of 2.5. The findings indicate relatively minor changes over time. We separated the radio galaxies into two groups: those hosted by inactive and star-forming galaxies, discovering that star-forming galaxies host the dominant population at high redshifts. In contrast, radio galaxies in inactive galaxies are affected by their host galaxies' mass, which is consistent with findings from our local universe. At lower redshifts, inactive radio galaxies dominate, but their numbers decline sharply, while their brightness increases. On the other hand, star-forming radio galaxies become more common, eventually dominating at most radio-luminosity levels by a redshift of 1. Moreover, radio galaxies hosted by star-forming galaxies are influenced by their cold gas supply, which is not the case for their inactive counterparts.

This paper introduces annular settling and output annular settling for nonlinear systems, and develops conditions for generalized Persidskii systems under bounded input. Specifically, conditions are derived for short-time stability, boundedness, annular settling, and output annular settling, which are verified through linear matrix inequalities. A practical example involving recurrent neural networks demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Determining the precise displacement of mechanical oscillators or microwave fields in any phase space direction is feasible by coupling them to ancilla qubits, which then convey the displacement information for measurement. However, quantifying such displacement in unknown directions has not been accomplished in such systems. A proposed hybrid setup for phase space displacement measurement combines oscillators and qubits, leveraging feasible Rabi interactions to outperform conventional methods. The sensitivity of this hybrid Rabi interferometer is found to be unaffected by thermal noise, making pre-cooling of the oscillator unnecessary. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the interferometer is robust against qubit dephasing and oscillator thermalization, outperforming alternative methods under various conditions.

Designers encounter difficulties when tasked with optimizing designs by combining parameters to achieve multiple objectives. Complex HCI design problems, characterized by numerous objectives and time-consuming evaluations, are particularly challenging. Design algorithms, such as model-based computational methods, aid designers by generating potential solutions, but require pre-existing models of the interaction domain. Black box methods, on the other hand, are adaptable but their efficacy for designers has not been thoroughly investigated. Most studies on human-in-the-loop approaches were conducted by researchers or end-users, leaving a question about their utility for designers. This paper investigates Bayesian optimization, an algorithmic method for guiding the design optimization process, which suggests potential solutions based on prior observations. A comparative study involving 40 novice designers, who were tasked with optimizing a 3D touch interaction technique, found that the optimizer facilitated exploration of a larger design space and yielded better solutions. However, participants guided by the optimizer reported lower agency, expressiveness, and creativity, while also experiencing reduced mental effort and a sense of disempowerment. The findings suggest that human-in-the-loop optimization can be beneficial for novice designers where autonomy is not crucial.

To analyze graded Frobenius algebras from a ring-theoretical standpoint, we establish and examine properties of quasi-Frobenius and Frobenius rings, their shifted variants, and their structures, focusing on their representations. We revisit key concepts, such as simple Artinian and semisimple rings, and derive graded versions of established results on radicals, finiteness conditions, and injectivity. A key finding is a structural characterization of (shifted) Frobenius rings.

Our thesis focuses on developing optimization methods for addressing distinct issues in quantum information theory. We start by outlining a method for calculating quantum state probabilities, which involves projecting onto intersecting planes defined by probability distributions and measurement operators. We then assess its efficiency, accounting for real-world errors, in terms of processing time and accuracy. Next, we introduce a method for verifying quantum entanglement, where given a set of paired measurement frequencies, we identify a Bell inequality that maximizes the gap between local hidden variable and quantum Bell inequality values. Finally, to analyze the quantum marginal problem, we propose an operator and develop an algorithm, which takes a set of quantum marginal values and eigenvalues as input and returns a density matrix, if one exists, consistent with the specified data.

Our investigation focuses on a flat FLRW model within the framework of $f(R,T)$-gravity, which incorporates both the quadratic variation in scalar curvature and the linear term of the stress-energy tensor. We found that this model exhibits late-time universe behavior, characterized by accelerated expansion, ultimately leading to a big rip. We then propose a model parameterized by the scale factor, which commences with a singularity at a point of zero volume, infinite energy density, and infinite temperature. This model is currently accelerating and will resemble the $\Lambda$CDM model in the distant future. Moreover, our proposed model behaves like quintessence dark energy at present and is consistent with standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology at late times.

Utilizing the holographic description of super Yang-Mills theory, which models a string in AdS space, we investigated the correlators of fields interacting with entangled quark and anti-quark pairs. We explored two scenarios where the string's endpoints are stationary and where they are uniformly accelerated, and found that in both cases, we can derive the two-point correlators exactly, allowing for all-time evolution. The accelerated string induces a two-sided AdS black hole geometry, effectively forming a wormhole, which may realize the ER=EPR conjecture. We found causality to be pivotal in determining the dispersion relation of particles and their mutual interaction. When two particles are causally disconnected, their dynamics become dissipative, independent of distance, and their mutual coupling diminishes over time, following a power law. Conversely, when causally connected, their dispersion relation becomes non-dissipative. We will also discuss our findings' implications for entangled particle dynamics and the ER=EPR conjecture.

A cosmological model has been investigated within the context of $f(R)$-gravity, which is characterized by a cubic equation in scalar curvature. Nonlinear terms within the $f(R)$ function are interpreted as energy derived from curvature-inspired geometry, leading to accelerating expansion and negative pressure. Numerical methods were employed to determine several key parameters. The model was validated by analyzing observational Hubble data and Pantheon data, consisting of 46 and 40 data points, respectively. A comprehensive examination of the model was conducted by analyzing plots of various dynamical parameters, specifically the deceleration parameter and Hubble parameter, which indicated accelerating expansion. A transition from deceleration to acceleration occurred at a redshift of approximately 0.694069, which is in line with $\Lambda$CDM. Furthermore, state finder analysis was conducted, and results indicated that the model is consistent with $\Lambda$CDM in late times.

Recent machine learning techniques have found success in machinery fault detection. 
However, their primary drawback is their lack of transparency due to their 'black box' operation. 
To address this, we introduce the Temporal Logic Neural Network (TLNN), where its neurons are based on logical statements. 
Notably, this network can be understood and interpreted through weighted signal temporal logic. 
By incorporating traditional neural network benefits, TLNN provides a logical explanation of its decision-making process, 
resulting in accurate and efficient fault diagnosis, while offering insightful explanations for its results.

When cooling a complex quantum system from a thermal state to its quantum critical point, our research explores how quickly adiabaticity is lost. We found that the number of excited particles, which measures how smoothly the system evolves, follows certain scaling laws depending on how quickly we cool it, and on its initial and final temperatures. These laws are generally applicable, controlled by the key characteristics of the quantum phase transition. We demonstrated our findings mathematically for a specific quantum system connected to heat reservoirs, and then argued that our results are true under broad conditions. Our research shows that quantum critical properties can be studied at any temperature, without changing the system's control parameters.

In our research, we show that by utilizing simple analog transmissions and match filtering, a network can replicate the functionality of an edge server in federated learning, thus enabling large-scale learning without the need for such a server. We also develop an adaptive training method, which enables user equipment to perform continuous local computing without being interrupted by global parameter uploads. Our approach leverages the full potential of user equipment processing capabilities. Through analysis, we establish convergence rates for our proposed schemes, revealing their efficiency. We found that, under Gaussian interference, our method achieves comparable convergence rates to traditional server-based federated learning. However, under heavy-tailed interference, our method is affected by its severity, slowing down its convergence. Nevertheless, our results indicate that parallelizing computation and communication can significantly reduce system runtime, especially in scenarios with high communication latency. Our findings are further supported by extensive simulation results.

This study focuses on generalized moment functions of higher order and their connection to established binomial-type functions, which have been explored across various complex structures. Building on our previous research, where we examined similar functions within commutative groups, we further develop our understanding by extending our analysis to hypergroups. Specifically, we provide a characterization of generalized moment functions within the context of a one-variable polynomial hypergroup, leveraging partial derivatives of composed polynomials and analytic functions. We also illustrate our approach by deriving an explicit formula for moment-generating functions up to rank two within the Tchebychev hypergroup.

We introduce GraphMoE, a new approach to learning generative models for random graphs, utilizing a neural network that is trained to mimic the statistical properties of graph classes. By estimating moment values, the network matches the distribution of these graph classes. Graphlets, subgraphs of limited size, are used as features for training. Taking random noise as input, the network generates vector representations for graph nodes, which are then transformed into realistic graphs through a kernel application. Experimental results demonstrate GraphMoE's capability to produce graphs resembling those from chemistry, medicine, and social networks, and its ability to deceive discriminator networks designed to differentiate between classes of random graphs.

Multi-purpose models are effective for addressing distinct tasks, but their practical applications are limited by their inability to handle multiple tasks and adapt to new domains. Recent advancements in instructional prompts have shown potential for improving task generalization, yet there is still a lack of systematic research on their impact in combination with multi-task learning, especially within the biomedical field. To bridge this gap, this study examines the effectiveness of instructional prompts for biomedical multi-task learning. We developed the BoX, a collection of 32 tasks for biomedical natural language processing across various categories. By utilizing this meta-dataset, we propose a unified model called In-BoXBART, which can learn all tasks without task-specific components. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to create a unified model for biomedical tasks and leverage instructions for achieving generalization across multiple tasks. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms single-task and multi-task baselines by significant margins, and also exhibits notable improvement in few-shot learning. Furthermore, our analysis reveals substantial room for improvement across tasks, indicating potential research directions for future study.

We investigate how the limiting distribution of the expression $\frac{L'}{L}(1/2+\epsilon,\chi_D)$ behaves as the fundamental discriminant $D$ takes on various values. Specifically, where $0<\epsilon<\frac12$ and $\chi_D$ denotes the associated real character, we analyze its limiting distribution and its convergence rate. By extension, our findings yield an asymptotic bound for the magnitude of $\left|\frac{L'}{L}(1/2+\epsilon,\chi_D)\right|$ for small values.

In recent hyperspectral unmixing research, there has been a growing use of deep learning, particularly through autoencoder architecture. We introduce a new architecture and use simulated ground truth for abundances to refine the 'unmixing network' optimization. An 'approximation network' is applied beforehand, which improves spatial correlation in abundances and is then used by the 'unmixing network' and'mixing network'. Our 'Guided Encoder-Decoder Architecture for Hyperspectral Unmixing with Spatial Smoothness' proposes using abundances from one-hot encoding, which are computed using the k-means algorithm without relying on prior hyperspectral unmixing methods. We also modify the standard autoencoder constraint by incorporating abundances from the 'unmixing network'. We then experiment with two pre-trained network variations. The 'GAUSS_blind' method concatenates the 'unmixing network' and'mixing network' to back-propagate errors, while 'GAUSS_prime' uses results from a signal processing method as pseudo-ground truth. Our results, using four experimental datasets, show that our architectures outperform or match existing hyperspectral unmixing algorithms from both deep learning and signal processing domains.

Investigating 2-2 scattering in four-dimensional spacetime within the Celestial framework, we re-express Celestial amplitudes using the crossing symmetric dispersion relation, transforming them into symmetric partial waves. These partial waves exhibit unwanted singularities in the complex Celestial variable, necessitating their removal in local theories. By applying null constraints, we obtain closed-form expressions, which in turn yield new bounds on partial wave moments, allowing for the assessment of low spin dominance in scalar theories. We identify a novel form of positivity present across a broad class of theories, proving that it only manifests in spin-0 dominated theories. By removing spurious singularities from crossing symmetric partial waves, known as Feynman blocks, and analyzing their behavior within the Celestial variable, we discover remarkable properties, including typical realness, utilizing Geometric Function Theory. Leveraging GFT techniques, we derive non-projective bounds on Wilson coefficients, expressed in terms of partial wave moments.

A recent surge in research has been focused on enhancing Knowledge Distillation (KD) by combining various techniques, including Contrastive Learning, Intermediate Layer Distillation, Data Augmentation, and Adversarial Training. Our study presents CILDA, a novel learning-based data augmentation method specifically designed for KD, which employs intermediate layer matching and contrastive loss to improve masked adversarial data augmentation. CILDA achieves state-of-the-art results on both the GLUE benchmark and out-of-domain evaluation.

Cuesta-Conway numbers, known as surreal numbers, are introduced through their normal forms, which are families of exponentials indexed by ordinals. They are derived from the reals and ordinals, extending their properties, and from these extensions, addition, multiplication, and a total order relation naturally follow. A sequence of real-closed fields is constructed, and through this process, a complete proof is provided for the known fact that surreal numbers form a totally ordered, commutative, and real-closed field.

Reinforcement learning has been increasingly used in controlled text generation tasks, such as unsupervised text style transfer, but its application is hindered by the challenge of sparse rewards. These rewards are only available once the entire text is generated, making training inefficient and prone to divergence. To address this issue, recent studies proposed reward-shaping strategies, but their impact has been minimal. Conversely, our proposed method introduces a new approach that offers dense rewards for each token, thereby enhancing performance. We evaluated our method in unsupervised text style transfer and found significant improvements, outperforming current state-of-the-art systems by 21% and 12% according to human and automatic evaluations respectively. A comparison with the 'roll-out strategy' showed that our method boosts style transfer quality by 22% and reduces training time by 7 times and sample requirements by 2.5 times.
In this article, we will provide a conclusive proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

A basic particle-in-a-box model has a straightforward Hamiltonian, given by $H=p^2$, within the bounded coordinate space $-b<q<b$, where $0<b<\infty$, using $2m=1$. Although extensively studied through canonical quantization, its simplicity has made it an ideal starting point for understanding quantum mechanics. However, recent investigations using affine quantization methods challenge previous results, particularly concerning quantization, and suggest a need to re-examine the particle-in-a-box system, which may involve more intricate eigenfunctions and eigenvalues.

Recent benchmark studies have revealed that, despite reported advancements, some subfields of machine learning have not made significant progress. A key reason for this stagnation is the irreproducibility of many comparative studies, primarily due to inadequate control of known sources of variability. These issues hinder independent verification of results. To address this, our study aims to synthesize and categorize the identified causes of irreproducibility, drawing from existing literature. We will present our findings, highlighting both the root causes and their implications, and propose three key areas for future investigation.

Through scientific discoveries, intricate connections are often revealed, frequently through simplification. However, applying deep learning to these findings has been impeded by the challenge of deciphering its results. To overcome this, researchers employed the Information Bottleneck framework, which analyzes relationships by balancing the accuracy and complexity of their approximations. By distributing these bottlenecks across multiple elements of the input, a new, groundbreaking method for interpretable deep learning emerged. Dubbed the Distributed Information Bottleneck, this innovation constrains and monitors the complexity of interactions within the system, thus simplifying its intricate workings without needing tailored data sets or neural networks. When applied to intricate systems, the Distributed IB offers profound insights by restricting and examining the information from different system components. Demonstrated through examples from applied mathematics and condensed matter physics, the Distributed IB has been successfully employed to disentangle the intricate workings of complex systems.

To evaluate the ability of NLP models to handle diverse, previously unseen tasks when provided with step-by-step instructions, we've developed Super-NaturalInstructions, a comprehensive benchmark featuring 1,616 unique tasks and their expert-created guidelines. These tasks, spanning 76 distinct categories, allow for thorough assessment of cross-task generalization under instruction-driven training and evaluation. We've also developed Tk-Instruct, a transformer-based model trained to understand and follow various in-context instructions. Results demonstrate Tk-Instruct outperforms current instruction-following models, including InstructGPT, by 9% on our benchmark, despite being significantly smaller. Additionally, our study examines how scaling parameters, such as task exposure, instance density, and model size, impact generalization. We envision our dataset and model will contribute to advancements in developing more versatile NLP models.

Research on newly discovered spin-orbit coupled states has sparked intense interest in certain transition metal systems, particularly those featuring iridate materials and α-RuCl3. By adjusting the balance between spin-orbit interaction and crystal field effects, scientists were able to create a new spin-orbital configuration characterized by Ising interactions. This breakthrough involved transforming the compound Li2RhO3 into Ag3LiRh2O6 through a specific chemical reaction, resulting in heightened crystal distortion and weakened spin-orbit coupling. Using mathematical modeling, researchers derived an explicit formula for the new spin-orbital configuration, which differs significantly from its conventional counterpart. Consequently, the material underwent a dramatic shift from being a spin-glass at 6 Kelvin to an antiferromagnet at 94 Kelvin, providing new avenues for exploring magnetic phase transitions.

A crucial obstacle in resolving time-dependent partial differential equations lies in developing computationally efficient solvers that are both accurate and stable. To tackle this challenge, we propose employing a graph neural network technique to devise efficient PDE solvers through machine learning, utilizing message-passing models. We begin by developing domain-agnostic features for PDE data, inspired by traditional PDE solvers, to achieve an efficient physical representation. Subsequently, we utilize graphs to represent PDE data on irregular meshes and demonstrate that message-passing graph neural networks can express governing equations, enabling the efficient learning of accurate solver methods for both linear and nonlinear PDEs. Moreover, our approach yields solvers that are independent of the initial geometry, indicating that the trained solver can effectively solve PDEs on different complex domains. Finally, we show that a recurrent graph neural network can identify a temporal sequence of solutions to a PDE.

Single photon emitters are often distinguished using Hanbury Brown and Twiss intensity interferometers, consisting of a beamsplitter and two correlated single photon detectors. However, their identification can be impeded when dealing with imperfect detectors and optics. Specifically, non-ideal detectors, particularly those with unequal detection efficiency, and high background noise levels, exceeding the true signal rate, can hinder accurate identification of single photon emitters.

We introduce a single-pixel imaging camera, known as the complementary detection and optimized Bernoulli modulation (CSPI) camera, capable of substantially mitigating the impact of external light interference in single-pixel imaging (SPI) applications. Numerical simulations confirm that when using binary coded patterns, the CSPI camera can reliably produce undisturbed images even under extreme fluctuation of background light, outperforming both SPI and differential SPI techniques. The successful implementation of CSPI cameras has the potential to significantly advance the practical applications of single-pixel imaging Lidar.

We explore advanced finite element techniques, specifically enriched unfitted and generalized finite element methods (GFEM), to tackle complex interface problems, including one-dimensional elliptic problems with discontinuous solutions and implicit or Robin-type interface conditions. A key challenge in developing these methods is creating enrichment functions that capture solution discontinuities without causing the condition number to rapidly increase. A new, linear stable generalized finite element method (SGFEM) has been developed using one enrichment function, and we extend this approach to arbitrary degrees using two straightforward, discontinuous, one-sided enrichment functions. We demonstrate optimal convergence in both the $L^2$ and broken $H^1$-norms, as well as at all nodes. To showcase the efficiency of SGFEM, we apply enriched linear, quadratic, and cubic elements to a multi-layer wall model for drug-eluting stents, which involves both zero-flux and implicit concentration interface conditions.

Stabilizer states in n-qubit systems are those that remain unchanged under specific transformations from the Pauli group. A group of unitary operations, known as the Clifford group, maps these stabilizer states to other stabilizer states, and can be generated using certain fundamental quantum gates. These gates create a complex network of relationships between stabilizer states, known as reachability graphs, which can be analyzed to understand their entropic properties. We explore these relationships, specifically those involving only two-qubit operations, and show how they evolve from two to four qubits. However, at four qubits, some stabilizer states exhibit entropic properties that cannot be explained by certain principles, marking a transition from predictable to complex behavior.

MultiEarth 2022, the inaugural competition, will assess deforestation in the Amazon rainforest under diverse conditions. This challenge seeks to establish a unified standard for processing and analyzing multimodal information and unite experts from earth science, environmental science, and multimodal learning to evaluate and compare different methods for deforestation estimation under standardized conditions. MultiEarth 2022 will consist of three sub-competitions: matrix completion, deforestation estimation, and image-to-image translation. This document outlines the competition guidelines, datasets, and evaluation criteria for each sub-competition. The MultiEarth 2022 challenge can be accessed at https://sites.google.com/view/rainforest-challenge.

Recent studies highlight the need to balance conflicting goals during model training, including reconciling factors such as accuracy and fairness, or different measures of fairness. These trade-offs are indicative of a broader class of multi-objective optimization problems, where optimization techniques strive to find optimal compromises between competing objectives. Our work begins by introducing a differentiable metric that allows for direct optimization of group fairness (particularly, achieving balance in accuracy across different groups) during model training. We then demonstrate two framework approaches for learning optimal parameters for different groups of neural classification models, using multi-objective optimization. We evaluate our approaches on the specific task of detecting hate speech, where previous studies have shown disparities in group fairness across speakers from different English dialects. Our empirical results, using convolutional, sequential, and transformer-based neural architectures, show better balance between accuracy and fairness compared to previous work. Moreover, our measure allows the Pareto optimization mechanism to ensure each architecture achieves its optimal balance between fairness and accuracy, given predefined error tolerance limits.

Tailoring the electronic structure of epitaxial graphene is achievable through an established technique known as intercalation. Furthermore, this method allows for the synthesis of thin layers of certain elements, which are typically unstable, due to their unique physical properties resulting from quantum confinement at their interfaces. Our work has resulted in the uniform synthesis of lead-intercalated, nearly independent, single-layer graphene on silicon carbide, characterized by being essentially neutral and exhibiting an exceptionally low concentration of positively charged carriers. Utilizing momentum microscopy, we were able to detect low-energy bands associated with metallic lead at the interface, and low-energy electron diffraction revealed a distinct periodicity relative to the graphene, indicating its interaction with lead. Our findings demonstrate the potential for creating new, heavy-element-based superconducting materials at the graphene-silicon carbide interface, offering opportunities for spin-orbit interactions and even two-dimensional superconductivity.

Conversational systems using retrieval-based models typically evaluate potential responses based on their similarity to vector representations of given dialogue contexts. However, solely using one specific text form of the multi-turn context can prevent models from learning adaptable representations for natural variations encountered during inference. To address this limitation, our proposed framework incorporates modified versions of dialogue contexts into its learning objectives. We incorporate contrastive learning as an auxiliary goal to learn resilient dialogue context representations that remain consistent despite perturbations created through our augmentation technique. Our experiments involve testing our framework on four benchmark datasets and show that it effectively integrates with existing data augmentation methods, significantly outperforming baseline models based on BERT. Furthermore, we introduce ConMix, a new data augmentation approach, which introduces token-level variations through random mixing of tokens from other contexts within the batch. Our proposed method surpasses previous data augmentation techniques, resulting in more robust dialogue representations that are less susceptible to common variations encountered during inference.

A promising approach to enabling robots to learn skilled manipulation is through imitation learning, which allows for skill acquisition without requiring extensive computational resources or precision-crafted rewards. Nevertheless, current imitation learning techniques rely on extensive data collection infrastructure and struggle to generalize beyond their training data. To overcome these limitations, researchers can collect additional data representing the full operational environment. This work explores the characteristics of supplementary demonstrations and their influence on performance, focusing on corrective and randomly-sampled demonstrations. Our investigation, involving a robot hand performing a pick-and-place task, demonstrates that corrective demonstrations significantly outperform randomly-sampled demonstrations when there are more additional demonstrations from the full distribution than original demonstrations from a restricted distribution. Conversely, when there are more original demonstrations, corrective and randomly-sampled demonstrations show no significant differences. Our findings reveal the underlying trade-off between collecting corrective demonstrations and their relative benefits. Additionally, inexpensive vision-based sensors, such as LeapMotion, can significantly reduce the cost of collecting demonstrations for skilled manipulation tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/GT-STAR-Lab/corrective-demos-dexterous-manipulation.

This paper presents the BLCU-ICALL system, which excelled in SemEval-2022 Task 1, particularly in the Definition Modeling subtrack. Our approach, based on a transformer architecture, successfully combines multiple embedding types using cross-attention and leverages gloss structure through a masking language model objective. To further enhance robustness, we employ a simple yet efficient ensemble strategy. Our system achieved outstanding results, ranking first in Italian, second in Spanish and Russian, and third in English and French. To facilitate reproducibility, our code is available at: https://github.com/blcuicall/SemEval2022-Task1-DM.

Open clusters play a vital role in understanding star formation, stellar evolution, and mapping our Galaxy's physical characteristics. Recent access to accurate large-scale star measurements has greatly reduced the difficulty of distinguishing open clusters from background stars. However, current studies are limited due to their reliance on visible light. To address this, we extended our open clusters' brightness ranges, incorporating near-infrared data from the VVV survey to supplement Gaia information. Our analysis of 37 clusters using machine learning and statistical models enabled us to distinguish clusters from background stars at near-infrared wavelengths. As a result, our study revealed around 47% more potential new members, based on their membership probability, thereby expanding our understanding of these clusters. This investigation is part of a larger series aiming to standardize near-infrared open cluster identification.

This survey presents advancements from roughly the past decade in tackling the intricacies of approximately solving constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) in the frameworks of streaming and sketching models of computation. We first outline several relevant outcomes, followed by concise descriptions of their proofs, focusing on elucidating the rationale behind the existence of a strict dichotomy for sketching algorithms operating within the subpolynomial space domain.

A planet's internal structure greatly influences its response to external gravitational forces, particularly in terms of its rotation. Specifically, the presence of a specific oscillation mode in the planet's fluid core can amplify its reaction to external forces at certain frequencies. This oscillation mode, referred to as the Free Core Nutation, is similar to another mode called the Spin-Over Mode, which occurs when the planet's fluid core oscillates freely. Through modeling, we've found that the Spin-Over Mode occurs when the forces acting on the planet's mantle are balanced, causing it to rotate steadily. Dissipation at the boundary between the planet's core and mantle can cause the Free Core Nutation to slow down and slightly change its frequency. Our research shows that this effect can be attributed to the close proximity of the Free Core Nutation frequency to the Spin-Over Mode, which in turn affects the planet's resonance quality. We explore the implications of this mechanism for other planets, including Mars, the Moon, and Earth's long-term evolution.

A cutting-edge approach in materials and life sciences, infrared hyperspectral imaging, has been hindered in its application to sub-diffraction nanoimaging due to its inefficient data acquisition methods. To address this limitation, researchers applied the mathematical concept of low-rank matrix reconstruction to enhance the efficiency of atomic force microscopy-based infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) hyperspectral nanoimaging. To validate its efficacy, they utilized Leishmania species, a significant target in life sciences, and successfully applied the mid-infrared spectral fingerprint window from 1300 to 1900 cm$^{-1}$, alongside a 220 nm step width. Through multivariate statistics, particularly hierarchical cluster analysis, they were able to identify chemically distinct regions. Notably, they reduced the data from 134 (x) $\times$ 50 (y) $\times$ 148 (spectral) measurements to only 5% and successfully recovered the full data set using low-rank matrix recovery. As a result, they observed significant agreement in cluster regions between full and reconstructed data cubes, ultimately reducing measurement time from over 14 hours to under one hour. This breakthrough has immense potential to enhance the practical application of hyperspectral nanoimaging in various settings, including academia and industry, particularly in the study of nano- and bio-materials.

We have calculated the thermal photon emissivity of the quark-gluon plasma at 250 MeV, using lattice QCD simulations and comparing our results to other theoretical models. Our study employed correlators from lattice QCD, which were used to derive the emissivity of thermal photons. We compared these to next-to-leading order perturbative QCD and infinite-coupling supersymmetric Yang-Mills models, and found good agreement. To refine our comparison, we applied the Backus-Gilbert method to model-independently analyze the spectral functions. Based on these findings, we used fit models to determine the emissivity at different frequencies. Our results show that at certain photon momenta, specifically around 0.8 GeV, the emissivity is constrained, and we obtained a differential photon emission rate per unit volume of approximately 2.2 x 10^-3 GeV.

Recent discoveries of flat bands in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) have led to significant research into strong correlation effects in electronic systems, specifically in Dirac materials. We find that the symmetry group protecting the Dirac cone in these materials dictates whether or not a Dirac band can be flattened by adjusting a small number of parameters. A newly developed criterion enables the calculation of the number of parameters necessary to make the Dirac velocity vanish, and is used to investigate band flattening in twisted bilayer graphene and three-dimensional topological insulators. Following this, we determine the symmetries under which the vanishing of the Dirac velocity leads to perfectly flat bands. Based on our analysis, additional model Hamiltonians are constructed to demonstrate perfectly flat bands at specific points in parameter space, including a model of coupled three-dimensional topological insulator surfaces and a quasi-crystalline extension of the chiral model of TBG.

We focus on controlling systems governed by nonlinear stochastic differential equations, and propose a new framework for path-wise control. A key innovation is the introduction of stochastic relative degree and a coordinate transformation, allowing the system to be represented in a stochastic normal form. This form facilitates the design of state-feedback controllers that can linearize and eliminate noise from the system. However, these ideal controllers are impractical due to their reliance on unmeasurable Brownian motion. Building on this idealized framework, we introduce a hybrid control architecture that achieves path-wise control in practice. By using periodic measurements of the state to compensate for noise, the hybrid controller can approximate ideal performance as the compensation period becomes infinitesimally small. Furthermore, we address the issue of asymptotic output tracking, providing solutions in both idealized and practical contexts. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a numerical example.

Observations of C/2017 K2 (PANSTARRS) using the Hubble Space Telescope showed distinct patterns in the properties of its coma, indicating the presence of sublimating, micron-sized water ice grains closer to the nucleus. As the distance from the nucleus increased, these patterns gave way to more stable, millimeter-sized grains, resulting in different reflectance and polarization properties. Near-infrared imagery from the Palomar Hale Telescope further supported this conclusion, showing no clear gradient in JHKs colors. These findings are consistent with expectations for Oort cloud comets and, in re-examining data from C/2012 S1 (ISON), researchers identified a reported polarimetric halo as an observational error.

Quantum computing offers significant potential for accelerating computationally intensive tasks, such as solving complex optimization problems involving numerous elements. Quantum algorithms can potentially speed up particle clustering in high-energy collider physics, notably in the case of jet formation. This study assesses the performance of quantum annealing methods in optimizing "thrust" in electron-positron collision events, using jet clustering as a benchmark. Our results show that quantum annealing can match classical methods and heuristics in terms of performance, albeit only after optimizing the annealing parameters. Conversely, comparable performance can be achieved through a combination of quantum and classical approaches, even without parameter tuning.

We introduce cross-view transformers, a highly efficient model for
semantic segmentation of maps from multiple camera views. This model uses
a sophisticated attention mechanism to learn a unified map representation
from various camera angles. Each camera view incorporates spatial
embeddings, accounting for its unique perspective, to facilitate seamless
transformation across views. A convolutional encoder and cross-view
transformer are used in tandem to produce accurate map semantic
segmentations. Notably, our model boasts simplicity, ease of parallel
processing, and real-time capabilities. Its performance surpasses current
standards, demonstrating 4x faster inference speeds, and can be accessed
via https://github.com/bradyz/cross_view_transformers.

Cellular functions, such as cell division and movement, are heavily influenced by intracellular protein patterns, leading to complex cell shape transformations. These transformations can, in turn, impact the behavior of pattern-forming proteins, creating an intricate feedback loop between cell shape and chemical dynamics. Despite computational studies, the underlying mechanisms are not yet fully understood, prompting an investigation into cell polarity on a one-dimensional, dynamic surface. By incorporating geometric concepts, equations governing mass-conserving reaction-diffusion systems are derived, revealing that cell shape changes can trigger pattern-forming instabilities, and distortions in membrane geometry can suppress or shift existing patterns. Using local equilibria theory, an onset criterion for pattern-forming instabilities linked to reaction-diffusion phase-space is established, leading to a diverse array of pattern phenomena, including oscillations, traveling and standing waves, not observed in fixed-shape systems. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that cell membrane geometry plays a significant role in controlling pattern formation in mass-conserving reaction-diffusion systems.

In natural language processing, euphemisms have been understudied despite their significant impact on polite and figurative speech. Investigating these phrases proves to be complex, primarily because they evolve over time and are open to interpretation regarding what constitutes a euphemism. A crucial first step in addressing this challenge lies in compiling and examining examples of euphemisms. This study introduces a collection of words and phrases possibly used euphemistically (PETs) paired with examples from the GloWbE corpus, and another subcollection of texts in which these PETs are used non-euphemistically. Analysis of the PETs reveals that they tend to diminish negative and offending sentiments, and human annotators' disagreement in categorizing PETs, partly attributed to their recognition as conventional, commonly accepted terms.
This paper examines the generalized Hyers-Ulam stability of the given reciprocal functional equation.

This research aims to achieve precise three-dimensional surface detection in smoothed particle hydrodynamics for fluid flows with open surfaces. A novel spatial technique is initially developed to boost the precision of identifying surface particles in intricate fluid dynamics. This technique locates surface particles by scanning globally within a cone area surrounding each particle, and marks a particle as a surface particle if a cone area devoid of adjacent particles is discovered. Subsequently, an efficient spatial technique is introduced, based on the initial one, to minimize computational costs. It involves identifying particles close to the surface using divergence analysis and then applying the spatial technique to pinpoint surface particles. The efficacy and reliability of the proposed technique are validated through testing on various model cases.

My research focuses on six novel observational tests of general relativity. First, I demonstrate that gravitational waves from merging supermassive black holes can cause a long-lasting increase in the distance between the Earth and the Moon, making the Moon slightly more unstable. This effect, albeit minuscule, can be detected using lunar ranging techniques. Second, I establish a universal limit imposed by general relativity on the energy flux from cosmological sources, depending on their redshift. Third, I investigate the feasibility of intergalactic travel using rockets, considering an alternative theory to dark matter, known as Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND), which alters inertia at very low accelerations. I show that, according to MOND, rockets might achieve efficient intergalactic travel. Fourth, I show that, in the context of MOND, the observed dipole of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) can originate from the primordial fluctuation amplitude at the cosmic horizon. Fifth, I demonstrate that the Milky-Way galaxy's gravitational potential can remove dark matter from its satellite galaxies through quantum tunneling. Sixth, I show that a charged particle can reach infinite energies by synchronizing its motion with a planar gravitational wave propagating in a uniform magnetic field, potentially resulting in electromagnetic afterglows near gravitational-wave sources.

The biadjoint scalar partial amplitude can be expressed as a single integral, resulting in a Global Schwinger Parameterization. This work extends to all partial amplitudes, utilizing a limiting procedure to incorporate indicator functions into the integrand. Applying the same limiting procedure yields an integral representation of $\phi^4$ amplitudes, where indicator functions convert to Dirac delta functions. These delta functions' support areas break down into $\textrm{C}_{n/2-1}$ regions, defined by the $q^{\rm th}$-Catalan number, and each region corresponds to a $m_{n/2+1}(\alpha,\mathbb{I})$ amplitude. A combinatorial description of these regions in terms of non-crossing chord diagrams is provided, and a general formula for $\phi^4$ amplitudes is proposed using the Lagrange inversion construction. Additionally, the exploration of $\phi^p$ theories reveals that their regions are represented by non-crossing $(p-2)$-chord diagrams, and the expansion of $\phi^p$ amplitudes in terms of $\phi^3$ amplitudes mirrors the structure of Green functions in terms of connected Green functions in the planar limit of $\Phi^{p-1}$ matrix models. Further, possible connections to recent constructions involving Stokes polytopes and accordiohedra are discussed.

A theoretical examination of the spatial characteristics of symmetric signals produced by degenerate four-wave mixing in a thin layer of two-level atoms exposed to Gaussian beams is provided. Accounting for the comprehensive spatial and spectral influences of relevant nonlinear susceptibilities, two notable phenomena are uncovered. Firstly, the combined power of the incident beams influences the transverse distribution of the four-wave mixing signals upon exiting the medium and their subsequent free propagation. Secondly, the spectral properties of the medium affect the longitudinal profile of the generated signals upon free propagation. These effects can be viewed as resulting from the saturation of regions with higher intensity and from a nonlinear contribution to the refractive index within the atomic medium. Additionally, these phenomena can exhibit symmetry between the signals, with induced asymmetries resulting from differences in detuning from resonance of the incident fields.

We introduce an approach to design metasurface apertures, enabling the creation of specified radiation patterns. A metasurface is composed of miniaturized, active metamaterial components, each behaving like an electric dipole. By leveraging holography, ideal polarizability distributions can be determined, and these can be converted into feasible distributions using established principles. However, actual metamaterial resonators are restricted in their polarizability, with their phase and magnitude intertwined, resulting in a 180-degree phase range. To circumvent these limitations, we propose a series of transformations from ideal to feasible polarizability distributions, effectively representing these in the complex plane. These transformations can be utilized to design metasurface antennas producing optimized beam patterns, thereby compensating for inherent resonator constraints.

Activity recognition in surgical videos is crucial for developing advanced devices and workflow monitoring systems. Given the variable lengths of surgeries, deep learning models typically comprise a two-stage setup, utilizing a backbone and temporal sequence model. This study explores numerous state-of-the-art backbones and temporal models to identify architectures that provide the highest performance in recognizing surgical activities. Initially, the models' performance is evaluated on a comprehensive dataset of over 800 surgery videos recorded in various clinical operating rooms. Subsequently, the models are assessed on the Cholec80 and Cataract-101 datasets, consisting of 80 and 101 videos, respectively. Through empirical analysis, the Swin-Transformer+BiGRU temporal model demonstrated excellent performance on both datasets. Finally, the adaptability of the model to new domains is examined by fine-tuning the model to a new hospital and applying an unsupervised domain adaptation approach.

The most accurate direct CDF W mass measurement of 80,433 $\pm$ 9 MeV significantly diverges from the Standard Model's predicted mass of 80,359.1 $\pm$ 5.2 MeV, at a 7σ difference. Although CDF used an outdated ResBos code, data-driven techniques in the analysis likely accounted for most of the corrections, and applying more accurate ResBos2 predictions at N$^3$LL+NNLO might decrease the measured mass by up to 10 MeV.

This research focuses on rectifying malfunctioning 3D objects, departing from earlier approaches that centered on passive perception systems to determine functionality from static objects. Instead, functionality is defined in relation to physical interactions between users and objects. Building upon human intuition, where mental simulations enable users to reason about object functionality and repair, we introduce FixIt, a dataset of approximately 5,000 inadequately designed 3D objects, accompanied by potential repair options. Our proposed solution, FixNet, emulates human mental simulations by combining perception and physical dynamics. This includes a perception module to analyze 3D point clouds, a physical dynamics module to simulate object responses to interaction, and a functionality module to assess object functionality and choose an optimal repair. Our results demonstrate FixNet significantly outperforms comparable models, and can effectively adapt to objects with analogous interaction types.

Researchers revise previous approaches to determine the CP-violating phase in lepton physics, utilizing modified versions of well-known mixing patterns. They incorporate small adjustments to these patterns, generating new mixing matrices, and convert them into a standard format. By analyzing these modified matrices in relation to known experimental data, they establish links between the CP-violating phase and other neutrino oscillation parameters. Using these findings, they constrain the possible range of the CP-violating phase and estimate its probability. Additionally, they explore future experiments' potential to test the modified scenarios and present an A4 symmetry model that aligns with one of these scenarios and matches current data.

A novel approach to acoustic transfer function (ATF) interpolation between spatial regions has been developed, considering both physical characteristics and directional configurations. Unlike conventional spatial ATF interpolation methods, which are mainly restricted to receiver locations, this new approach enables ATF estimation in both source and receiver regions from a finite set of measurements. By incorporating directional weighting into the reproducing kernel Hilbert space and associated kernel function, the interpolation accuracy can be significantly enhanced. Furthermore, optimal hyperparameter selection techniques for the kernel function have been explored. Simulation results show that the proposed method outperforms previous methods lacking directional weighting.

In proton-proton collisions at various energy levels, from 13 to 500 TeV, we investigate the anticipated mass distributions of dijet resonances originating from excited quarks. By examining both the generator and experimental perspectives, we pinpoint the influences of excited quark natural width, proton parton momentum distributions, radiation, and experimental resolution within these distributions. Our findings are presented in the form of both differential and cumulative probability distributions of dijet mass and signal acceptance within a mass window centered on each resonance. Significantly, for a range of resonance masses between 10% and 50% of the energy, the mass distributions and acceptance rates exhibit remarkable universality, remaining relatively unchanged despite variations in resonance mass and energy. This research supports previous work, specifically the 2021 Snowmass study, on detecting dijet resonances in proton-proton colliders.

We introduce an unsupervised, hierarchical scene representation for generative models, comprising organized "blobs" of features in a depth-ordered arrangement. Our approach, implemented within a generative adversarial network, enables the model to differentiate and arrange these blobs to capture scene structure and relationships. Despite the absence of supervision, our method exhibits emergent behavior, facilitating scene manipulation and parsing, and yielding comparable or superior results to state-of-the-art models, such as StyleGAN2, in evaluating scene generation quality.

Manual analysis of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals can be labor-intensive and inefficient, prompting the exploration of automated solutions through machine learning (ML) classification. By leveraging ML models to analyze heartbeat patterns, potential abnormalities can be detected. However, the lack of transparency in Deep Learning applications in healthcare can hinder their adoption. This thesis aims to develop and compare Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) classifiers, in addition to shallow models, to assess their performance and interpretability. Various interpretability methods, including global and local techniques, are employed to analyze model decisions and patterns. Specifically, Partial Dependence Plots, Shapley Additive Explanations, Permutation Feature Importance, and Gradient Weighted Class Activation Maps (Grad-Cam) are utilized to examine the behavior of time-series ML models in ECG rhythm classification. Our investigation focuses on Grad-Cam, a local interpretability technique, to determine its effectiveness in explaining predictions of CNN and LSTM models. Through rigorous evaluation and statistical analysis, including K-Fold cross-validation and Leave Groups Out techniques, we found that Grad-Cam is the most effective interpretability method. Our results suggest that all high-performing classifiers primarily focus on the QRS complex of the ECG rhythm when making predictions.

Recently, researchers introduced "No-Clash Teaching" or "NC-Teaching", an optimal teaching model. This model satisfies Goldman and Matthias' collusion-freeness condition and outperforms other collusion-free teaching models. A significant finding is that any concept class with an NC-teaching dimension of d and n elements can have at most (2^d * (n choose d)) concepts. Key results in the paper include characterizing maximum concept classes of NC-teaching dimension 1 and discovering a family of classes with logarithmic recursive teaching dimensions, despite having an NC-teaching dimension of 1. Additionally, the paper reduces an existing upper bound on concepts by a factor of order sqrt(d) and verifies the new bound using Johnson graphs and maximum subgraphs.

Dark matter is viewed as a collection of heavy particles, behaving in a collision-prone, gravitationally interacting, and energy-quantum exchanging manner. A novel, non-relativistic quantum framework is proposed to model dark matter, rooted in an equation recently formulated for a chargeless, uncharged, and unencumbered particle. This framework elucidates the quantum phenomena occurring within the particles, outlines the requisite energy quantum wavelength, establishes limits on the mass of dark matter particles, and foresees the existence of a detectable gravitational wave background tied to dark matter clusters.

The concept of optical excitons, photo-excited electron-hole pairs within crystals, is widely used to understand and model various phenomena in semiconductors. Optical excitons exhibit properties such as condensation, diffusion, and recombination, however, these properties are based on an initial theoretical model of excitons as distinct particles. This paper presents an alternative perspective, demonstrating how electron-phonon interactions break down initial optical excitons into elemental excitons, distinct from the initial model. This finding is achieved within a many-body perturbation theory framework, starting from an interacting electronic Hamiltonian, and applied to realistic systems such as monolayer MoS$_2$ and MoSe$_2$ using first-principles methods. As a result, the optical excitons are found to gradually lose their initial structure, leading to a homogeneous broadening of absorption peaks, and eventually evolve into elemental excitons, the true intrinsic excitations of the interacting system.

A new formalism in knowledge integration, called standpoint logic, offers a way to reason with various perspectives, allowing them to coexist without forced unification. This paper presents formal systems, or proof methods, for handling multiple viewpoints, and shows how to automate decision-making with algorithms. To make these algorithms run efficiently, the paper introduces a new technique, "coloring," which involves assigning colors to formula components and then running the algorithm. This method enables determining the validity of multiple perspectives in a certain amount of time, and when valid, generates a complete explanation, or when invalid, creates a model of why it is incorrect.

In magnetic memory technology, electric currents can manipulate magnetic properties to alter data. This process typically involves layered structures comprising ferromagnetic and spin-injection layers. One way to inject spins is through a non-magnetic layer with significant spin Hall effects. Researchers have now successfully created a single, two-dimensional magnetic bit in MoTe2/WSe2, leveraging the material's inherent magnetism and Berry curvature. This AB-stacked material can host magnetic properties at specific density levels. When an electric current is applied, the material shows hysteresis in electrical resistance, and superconducting quantum interference device imaging reveals individual magnetic domains reversing due to the applied current. This phenomenon aligns with the material's spin accumulation near specific energy levels, suggesting that intrinsic properties drive the observed effects. This breakthrough in MoTe2/WSe2 and similar materials enables low-density control of magnetic properties.

Measurements of single, double, and triple-differential cross-sections have been taken for top-quark pairs produced in high-energy proton-proton collisions, detected by the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The top quarks were identified through their decay into large-radius jets, with the most energetic jet having a momentum of over 500 GeV. After accounting for detector effects, the observed data yielded a particle-level cross-section of approximately 331 fb, with uncertainties of 3% statistical and 39% systematic. This result is roughly 20% lower than predictions from Powheg+Pythia, which have next-to-leading-order accuracy, yet remains within theoretical uncertainties. Additionally, parton-level cross-sections have been determined, removing the effects of top-quark decay, parton showering, and hadronization, to enable comparison with more precise calculations. At the parton level, the measured cross-section of approximately 1.94 pb shows excellent agreement with next-to-next-to-leading-order predictions of 1.96 pb. Most NLO models demonstrate reasonable consistency with differential cross-sections, whereas NNLO calculations exhibit better agreement with data. Finally, the differential cross-sections have been analyzed within the Standard Model effective field-theory framework, leading to constraints on Wilson coefficients of several four-fermion operators.

In this work, we explore the concept of teleporting a single qubit within a complex, strongly interacting quantum system, facilitated by local measurements and scrambling operations applied to a limited subset of qubits. Contrary to traditional methods, our demonstration shows that teleportation can be achieved in the 2D XY model without requiring a duplicate of the system and reversing time. This long-range entanglement necessary for teleportation is created from specific, unique eigenstates within the model, referred to as "rainbow scars." A particular protocol for generating this highly entangled state involves evolving an initial unentangled state and applying iterative, controlled measurements to just two qubits, incorporating feedback to optimize the process.

Legged robots experience significant difficulties when replicating agile maneuvers such as quick acceleration and sharp turns in unstructured environments. A newly developed end-to-end learning-based control system successfully maximizes agility in the MIT Mini Cheetah, reaching speeds of up to 3.9 m/s. This control system efficiently navigates uneven surfaces such as grass, ice, and gravel, and effectively handles disruptions. It uses a neural network trained in simulation via reinforcement learning, and successfully transitions to real-world applications. Two crucial components of the control system are (i) an adaptive learning strategy for adjusting velocity commands and (ii) an online identification method for transferring simulated data to real-world environments, building upon existing knowledge. Videos showcasing the robot's performance can be found at: https://agility.csail.mit.edu/

Digital health passes, such as the New York Excelsior Pass, offer a viable way to achieve certain benefits of "true elimination" COVID-19 strategies, which focus on complete case elimination rather than disease progression control. However, existing implementations of digital health passes rely on region-specific control and central storage of sensitive health data, creating barriers to widespread adoption across jurisdictions with incompatible data systems and inadequate patient privacy controls.
